<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\ 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rmfamily(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item In order to be able to include Boolean and monotone
    products and some other examples (Section~\ref{exaspread})
    we do not a priori assume the unitality. In some examples $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are naturally unital; then we also assume that $\varphi$ is also unital, i.e., $\varphi(1_{\mathcal{A}})=1_{\mathcal{B}}$ and also that involved subalgebras of $\mathcal{A}$ contain the unit of $\mathcal{A}$. 
\item 
Usually the involved algebras are $\ast$-algebras and the linear maps satisfy positivity.  
However positivity is not essential here and we stick to the algebraic
$\mathcal{B}$-valued setting, which allows to include the interesting
example of Lie polynomials in Section~\ref{sec:freeLiealg}. 



\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- defi-1: body_md -->
\label{def:spreaded}Let $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ be a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*., leftmargin=1cm]
 \item A \emph{spreadability system} for $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ is a triplet
  $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i=1}^\infty)$ satisfying the
  following properties:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*)]
 \item $(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi})$ is a $\mathcal{B}$-valued ncps.

 \item $\iota^{(i)}: \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{U}$ is a homomorphism
 such that $\varphi = \tilde{\varphi} \circ \iota^{(i)}$ for
  each $i \geq 1$. For simplicity, $\iota^{(i)}(X)$ is denoted by $X^{(i)}$, $X \in
  \mathcal{A}$, and we denote by $\mathcal{A}^{(i)}$ the image
  of $\mathcal{A}$ under $\iota^{(i)}$.
 \item The identity
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:spreadability}
    \tilde{\varphi}(X_1^{(i_1)}X_2^{(i_2)}\cdots X_n^{(i_n)}) = \tilde{\varphi}(X_1^{(h(i_1))}X_2^{(h(i_2))}\cdots X_n^{(h(i_n))}) 
  \end{equation}
  holds for any $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{A}$, any $i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_n \in
  \mathbb{N}$ and any \emph{order preserving} map $h:\{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_n\}
  \to \mathbb{N}$, that is, $i_p < i_q$ implies $h(i_p)<h(i_q)$.
\end{enumerate}
\item A triplet $\mathcal{E}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i=1}^\infty)$ is called an
 \emph{exchangeability system} if, in addition to (i), (ii) above, eq.\
 (\ref{eq:spreadability}) holds for any $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{A}$, any $i_1,
 i_2, \ldots, i_n \in \mathbb{N}$ and any \emph{permutation}
 $h \in \mathfrak{S}_\infty:=\bigcup_{n\geq 1}\mathfrak{S}_n$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\  
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=1cm]
\item In some examples where $\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}, \varphi$ are unital, the extended algebra $\mathcal{U}$ is also unital and $\iota^{(i)}$ are unit-preserving. To be specific, this applies to the tensor and free spreadability systems in Section \ref{exaspread} and the unshuffle spreadability system in Section \ref{sec:freeLiealg}.  
    \item It is easy to see that condition (\ref{eq:spreadability}) can be rephrased as follows:
    \begin{equation*}
(\iota^{(1)}, \iota^{(2)},\dots)
      \overset{d}{=} (\iota^{(n_1)}, \iota^{(n_2)},\dots)
    \end{equation*}
    for any strictly increasing sequence $(n_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. This
    is the definition given in \cite{Koe10}.

   \item It is straightforward to extend the definition of exchangeability
    systems (resp., spreadability systems) from  $\mathbb{N}$
    to an arbitrary set (resp., arbitrary totally ordered set).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- defi-2: body_md -->
\ 
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item 
    Using the concept of kernel partition from Definition~\ref{app:def:kernelpartition} the condition of spreadability
    \eqref{eq:spreadability} 
    is equivalent to the requirement that
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:phiXi1i2=phiXj1j2}
      \tilde\varphi(X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots X_n^{(i_n)}) = \tilde\varphi(X_1^{(j_1)} X_2^{(j_2)} \cdots X_n^{(j_n)})
    \end{equation}
    holds whenever the kernels
    coincide, i.e.,  $\kappa(i_1,i_2, \ldots, i_n) =
    \kappa(j_1,j_2,\ldots,j_n)$,
    see Definition~\ref{app:def:kernelpartition}.
    That is, the expectation (\ref{eq:spreadability}) 
    only depends on the ordered kernel set partition  $\kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)$.
    Thus for every ordered set partition $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ 
    we can define a multilinear functional
    $\varphi_\pi\colon \mathcal{A}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ by choosing any representative sequence
    $(i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_n)$ with $\kappa(i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_n)=\pi$ and setting
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:phipi}
      \varphi_{\pi}(X_1, X_2, \ldots,X_n)=\tilde{\varphi}(X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots X_n^{(i_n)}). 
    \end{equation}
    The invariance \eqref{eq:phiXi1i2=phiXj1j2} ensures that
    this definition is consistent and does not depend on the choice of the representative. 

\item 
This generalizes the corresponding notions from exchangeability systems \cite{L04}:
given an exchangeability system $\mathcal{E}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i=1}^\infty)$, we can define a multilinear functional $\varphi_\pi$, 
this time for any set partition $\pi \in \mathcal{P}_n$,   
\begin{equation*}
\varphi_{\pi}(X_1, X_2, \ldots,X_n)=\tilde{\varphi}(X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots X_n^{(i_n)}), 
\end{equation*}
where $(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)$ is any representative such that $\overline{\kappa}(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)=\pi$,  see Definition \ref{app:def:kernelpartition}. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The algebra $\mathcal{U}$ and the homomorphisms $(\iota^{(i)})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ of a
spreadability system can always be chosen to be the tensor algebra of the
copies of $\mathcal{A}$ (see \eqref{eq:coproduct} below) with the natural
embeddings, respectively, in the following sense.
Given a spreadability system $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i=1}^\infty)$ for a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$, we set $\hat{\mathcal{U}} := \bigsqcup_{i=1}^\infty\mathcal{A}_i$ where $\mathcal{A}_{i}$ are copies of $\mathcal{A}$ and set $\hat\iota^{(i)} \colon \mathcal{A} =\mathcal{A}_i \to \hat{\mathcal{U}}$ to be the natural embeddings. Then we can define $\hat \varphi \colon \hat{\mathcal{U}}  \to \mathcal{B}$ by setting
\[
\hat \varphi (\hat\iota^{(i_1)}(X_1)  \hat\iota^{(i_2)}(X_2)  \cdots \hat\iota^{(i_n)}(X_n)) := \tilde{\varphi} (X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots X_n^{(i_n)}) 
\]
for every $i_1, i_2,\dots, i_n$ with $i_k \ne i_{k+1}~(k\in[n-1])$ and
$X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n \in \mathcal{A}$, giving rise to the spreadability system $\hat
\mathcal{S}=(\hat{\mathcal{U}}, \hat \varphi, (\hat \iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ for $(\mathcal{A},
\varphi)$. Now $(\hat\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1}\overset{d}{=} (\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1}$ and
thus replacing $\mathcal{S}$ with $\hat\mathcal{S}$ does not change basic results; in
particular, the cumulants for $\mathcal{S}$ and for $\hat \mathcal{S}$ are identical, see
Theorem \ref{thm:mc}.  



In the majority of the examples below we choose $\mathcal{U}$ to be the tensor algebra,
in a few cases however, it is more natural to choose another $\mathcal{U}$.
A notable exception is the case of unital algebras, where 
the unital free product $\ast_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \mathcal{A}$ and the infinite tensor product
$\bigotimes_{i\in \mathbb{N}} \mathcal{A}$ are more convenient.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
For $d=1$ a binary operation $\operatorname*{\odot}$ satisfying conditions \eqref{eq:bifunctor}--\ref{U3} and \ref{U6} is called a \emph{quasi-universal product}  in \cite{Muraki:2002:five}. (Note that \eqref{eq:bifunctor} easily follows from \ref{U6}).
  On the other hand, a binary operation $\operatorname*{\odot}$ satisfying conditions \eqref{eq:bifunctor}--\ref{U3} is called a \emph{natural product} \cite{M03}.
 The main result of \cite{M03} is that \ref{U6} follows from \eqref{eq:bifunctor}--\ref{U3}, i.e., a natural product is a quasi-universal product.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:multiface} A more general setup was discussed in
  \cite{ManzelSchurmann:2016:noncommutative}, where the algebras are allowed to
  have an additional structure of \emph{faces}. The theory of cumulants is also
  developed in \cite{ManzelSchurmann:2016:noncommutative} for universal
  products with multistates and multifaces.  It seems that some modifications
  are needed in order to adapt the notion of
  spreadability system to the structure of faces but this issue is not discussed in the present paper.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- defi-3: body_md -->
\label{defi:universal_independence}  Let $d \in\mathbb{N}$ and $\operatorname*{\odot}$ be
  a universal product for $\operatorname{AlgP}_d$ satisfying conditions \ref{U1} and
  \ref{U2}. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an algebra and $\varphi = (\varphi^1, \dots,
  \varphi^d)$ be a tuple of $\mathbb{C}$-linear functionals on $\mathcal{A}$.  


\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item A sequence $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in [p]}$ of subalgebras of $\mathcal{A}$ is said to be \emph{$\operatorname*{\odot}$-independent} if the identity
 \[
\varphi^j \circ \tilde{\bigsqcup_{i\in[p]}}\gamma_i = \left[\operatorname*{\odot}_{i\in [p]} (\varphi\circ \gamma_i) \right]^j   \quad \text{on}\quad \bigsqcup_{i\in [p]} \mathcal{A}_i,  
 \]
 holds for all $j\in[d]$, where  $\gamma_i\colon \mathcal{A}_i \hookrightarrow \mathcal{A}$ is the embedding for $i\in [p]$ and $\tilde\sqcup_{i\in[p]}\gamma_i$ is the canonical arrow $\sqcup_{i\in[p]} \mathcal{A}_i \to \mathcal{A}$.   
 
If we further assume \ref{U6} the above definition is equivalent to the
requirement that for any  $n \in \mathbb{N}, i_1, i_2, \dots, i_n \in [p], X_k \in
\mathcal{A}_{i_k}~(k \in[n])$ we have  
\begin{equation}\label{eq:univ_calculation}
\varphi^j(X_1 X_2 \cdots X_n) =  \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{P}_n\\ \sigma \le \bar\pi}} \sum_{f\colon\, \sigma \to [d]} u^j (\sigma, f; \pi) \prod_{S \in \sigma} \varphi^{f(S)}(X_S),    \qquad j \in [d]. 
\end{equation}
 
\item  For an arbitrary totally ordered set $I$,
 a family of subalgebras $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ is called $\operatorname*{\odot}$-independent
 if any finite subfamily is  $\operatorname*{\odot}$-independent in the sense above.
 If the universal product $\operatorname*{\odot}$  in addition satisfies \ref{U4}
 then one can define  $\operatorname*{\odot}$-independence for a family of subalgebras $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ with \emph{any index set $I$} because one can define $\operatorname*{\odot}_{i\in I} (\varphi\circ \iota^{(i)})$ for any index set $I$. 
 
\item A family $(S_i)_{i \in I}$ of subsets of $\mathcal{A}$ with totally ordered index set $I$ is said to be $\odot$-independent if the family of subalgebras $\mathcal{A}_i$ generated by $S_i$ is $\odot$-independent. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-3 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
More examples may be extracted from associative universal products in \cite{BLS96,H10} for $d=2$ or $d=3$, but we omit them here.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- defi-4: body_md -->
\label{defi:universal} Let $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i \geq 1})$ be
  a spreadability system for a $\mathbb{C}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$.   For a set partition $\pi\in\mathcal{P}_n$ we define a multiplicative extension
  $\varphi_{(\pi)}$ of $\varphi$ by setting
  \begin{align} \label{eq:multiplicative}
    &\varphi_{(\pi)}(X_1,X_2,\ldots, X_n) :=\prod_{P\in \pi} \varphi(X_P) \quad \text{for}\quad  X_1, X_2,\dots, X_n \in \mathcal{A},
  \end{align}
  where we used notation \eqref{product}  for the ordered product $X_P$.  



 Then $\mathcal{S}$ is said to have a \emph{calculation rule} if there exists a family of complex numbers
  $\mathbf{C}= \{s(\sigma; \pi)\in\mathbb{C}: n \in \mathbb{N}, \pi\in \mathcal{OP}_n, \sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n, \sigma \leq
  \bar{\pi}\}$ such that the equality
\begin{equation}\label{eq:calculation_rule1}
\varphi_\pi=\sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n,\\ \sigma \leq \bar{\pi}}} s(\sigma; \pi) \, \varphi_{(\sigma)}
\end{equation}
holds as functionals on $\mathcal{A}^n$ for all $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Note that we can always take $s(\{1\}; (1))=1 $ because of $\tilde \varphi \circ \iota^{(i)} = \varphi$.
<!-- end defi-4 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=1cm]
    \item []
    \item 
 It is straightforward to see that a spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_\odot^1$
 constructed from a universal product $\odot$ on $\operatorname{AlgP}_1$ subject to axioms
 \ref{U1}, \ref{U2} and \ref{U6} has a calculation rule with $s(\sigma;
 \pi):=u^1(\sigma; \pi)$ (where $f$ is omitted because there is a unique
 $f\colon \sigma \to [1]$).  

\item  
Actually we can construct such a spreadability system for any given family of constants  $\mathbf{C} =\{s(\sigma; \pi)\in\mathbb{C}: n \in \mathbb{N}, \pi\in \mathcal{OP}_n, \sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n, \sigma \leq
  \bar{\pi}\}$ with  $s(\{1\}; (1))=1 $ and any given $\mathbb{C}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},
  \varphi)$. Let $\mathcal{U}$ be the coproduct (i.e., the tensor algebra) of the
  countable copies of $ \mathcal{A}$ in the category of associative algebras and 
  $\iota^{(i)}\colon \mathcal{A}\to \mathcal{U}$ the natural embedding as the $i$th component. Then we can define a linear functional $\tilde{\varphi}$ on $\mathcal{U}$ as follows: for each tuple $X_j \in \mathcal{A}~(1 \le j \le n)$ and indices $i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $i_k \ne i_{k+1}$ ($k\in[n-1]$) we set 
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:calculation_rule}
  \tilde \varphi (X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots X_n^{(i_n)}) := \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n,\\ \sigma \leq \bar{\kappa}(i_1,\dots, i_n) }} 
             s(\sigma; \kappa(i_1,\dots, i_n)) \, \varphi_{(\sigma)} (X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n). 
  \end{equation}
The fact that the value of \eqref{eq:calculation_rule} depends only on the partition $\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)$ induced by the sequence $(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n)$ yields that $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{C}}:= (\mathcal{U}, \tilde\varphi, (\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ is indeed a spreadability system.  
\item 
Muraki's example \cite{Muraki:private} yields a spreadability system with
calculation rule coming from a nonassociative universal product.
The V-monotone spreadability system is also such an example. We will investigate other instructive examples later in Examples \ref{exa:nonassociative0} and  \ref{exa:nonassociative}. 

\item 
 It is worth mentioning that there are spreadability
 systems without calculation rules. For instance, the algebra generated by left and right creation operators acting
 on $q$-Fock space gives rise to an exchangeability system
 \cite{Lehner:2005:cumulants3}, but it was shown in \cite{LeeuwenMaassen:1996:obstruction}
 that in this case the individual distributions of independent elements with respect to the vacuum expectation 
 is not sufficient to determine the joint distribution
 with respect to $(\varphi_\pi)_{\pi}$,
 and in particular there is no ``$q$-convolution''.  The c-monotone spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\rm CM}$ also does not have a calculation rule since the evaluation of $\varphi_\pi$ depends on both $\varphi$ and $\psi$ in general.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- defi-5: body_md -->
\label{def:exchangeableindependence}   
   Let $\mathcal{E}=(\mathcal{U},\tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ be an exchangeability system for a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$.  Let $I\subseteq \mathbb{N}$. 
  
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item Subalgebras $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{A}$ are said to be
  \emph{$\mathcal{E}$-independent} if for any tuple of indices $(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)\in I^n$, any tuple of random variables $(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)$ with $X_j\in \mathcal{A}_{i_j}$ and any set partition $\pi\in\mathcal{P}_n$, we have  
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:E-indep}
  \varphi_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) = \varphi_{\pi\wedge \bar{\kappa}(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n). 
  \end{equation}


\item Subsets  $(S_i)_{i \in I}$ of $\mathcal{A}$  are said to be
 \emph{$\mathcal{E}$-independent} if the algebras $\mathcal{A}_i$ generated by 
 $S_i$ are 
 $\mathcal{E}$-independent. In particular, a family
 $
 \bigl(
 (X_1(i),X_2(i),\dots,X_n(i))
 \bigr)_{i\in I}$ of random vectors
 is said to be
 \emph{$\mathcal{E}$-independent} if the subalgebras $\mathcal{A}_i$
 generated by its respective entries  $\{X_1(i),X_2(i), \dots, X_n(i)\}$
 are $\mathcal{E}$-independent.  
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-5 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
In the case where $\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{U}$ and $\varphi,
  \iota^{(i)}$ are unital,
  it is more natural to assume that the subalgebras $\mathcal{A}_i$ contain the unit
  of $\mathcal{A}$.
  The same applies to Definition \ref{def:S-independence}.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- defi-6: body_md -->
\label{def:S-independence}
  Let $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U},\tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ be a spreadability system for a given
  $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$. Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. 
  
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), leftmargin=1cm]
\item  A sequence of subalgebras $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{A}$ is said to be
  \emph{$\mathcal{S}$-independent} if for any tuple of indices
  $(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)\in I^n$, 
  any tuple of random variables $(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)$
  with $X_j\in  \mathcal{A}_{i_j}$
  and any ordered set partition $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$, we have
  \begin{equation}\label{S-indep} 
  \varphi_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) = \varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n).  
  \end{equation}
  
\item A sequence of subsets $(S_i)_{i \in I}$ is said to be
\emph{$\mathcal{S}$-independent} if the sequence  of subalgebras $\mathcal{A}_i$ generated by $S_i$ is $\mathcal{S}$-independent. 
In particular, a sequence of random vectors $((X_1(i),X_2(i),\dots,X_n(i)))_{i\in I}$ is said to be \emph{$\mathcal{S}$-independent} if the sequence of subalgebras $\mathcal{A}_i$ generated by $\{X_1(i),X_2(i),\dots, X_n(i)\}$ is $\mathcal{S}$-independent. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-6 -->
<!-- exa-1: body_md -->
For two subalgebras $\mathcal{S}$-independence reads as follows.
A pair of subalgebras
$(\mathcal{A}_1, \mathcal{A}_2)$ of $\mathcal{A}$ is
$\mathcal{S}$-independent if the following condition holds.
Given elements $X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n\in \mathcal{A}_1\cup \mathcal{A}_2$,
let $\rho=(B_1,B_2)$ be an ordered set partition of the index set $[n]$ such that
$X_i\in \mathcal{A}_1$ for $i\in B_1$ and $X_i\in \mathcal{A}_2$ for $i\in B_2$.
Then for any ordered set partition $\pi\in \mathcal{OP}_n$ we have
$$
\varphi_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = \varphi_{\pi\rfloor_{B_1}\pi\rfloor_{B_2}}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n).  
$$
<!-- end exa-1 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{E}=(\mathcal{U},\tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ be an
exchangeability system for a given $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$. It can be
regarded as a spreadability system and we denote it by  $\mathcal{S}$.  Then, obviously,  a sequence of subalgebras $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathcal{E}$-independent in the sense of Definition  \ref{def:exchangeableindependence} if and only if it is $\mathcal{S}$-independent in the sense of Definition \ref{def:S-independence}.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*., leftmargin=5ex]
   \item []
   \item 
With the notation introduced in Definition~\ref{def:dot} below, 
equation (\ref{S-indep}) may be rewritten as   
  $$
  \varphi_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) = \varphi_{\pi}(X_1^{(i_1)},X_2^{(i_2)},\dots,X_n^{(i_n)}).  
  $$
This condition means that the random vectors $(X_k)_{k\in [n]}$ and
$(X_k^{(i_k)})_{k\in [n]}$ have the same ``distribution'' with respect to
$(\varphi_\pi)_\pi$.  This is compatible with the concept of spreadability,
which is to regard the sequence $(\iota^{(j)}(\mathcal{A}))_{j \in I}$ as
independent copies $\mathcal{A}$ constructed in $(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi})$. 
\item 
An alternative natural definition of $\mathcal{S}$-independence would be to require the simplified condition that for any $(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)\in I^n$ and any 
 $X_j\in  \mathcal{A}_{i_j}, j \in [n]$, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weaker}
  \varphi (X_1 X_2  \cdots X_n) = \tilde\varphi(X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots X_n^{(i_n)}), 
\end{equation}
i.e., requiring \eqref{S-indep} only for $\pi =\hat1_n$.
In fact, for the spreadability systems associated with  a large class of
universal products,
\eqref{eq:weaker} implies the $\mathcal{S}$-independence, see Proposition
\ref{prop:equivalence_independences}.
In general however, condition \eqref{eq:weaker} does not imply $\mathcal{S}$-in\-de\-pen\-den\-ce, see Example \ref{exa:nonassociative0}. 
\item  In the case of exchangeability, $\mathcal{E}$-independence is equivalent to the
vanishing of mixed cumulants (see Proposition \ref{prop:mixedvanish}).


  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:equivalence_independences}  Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\operatorname*{\odot}$ be a universal product in the category $\operatorname{AlgP}_d$ satisfying \ref{U1}, \ref{U2} and \ref{U6}. Let $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi^1,\varphi^2, \dots, \varphi^d)$ be an object in $\operatorname{AlgP}_d$ and $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of subalgebras of $\mathcal{A}$ with $I\subseteq \mathbb{N}$. Then $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}$ is $\odot$-independent if and only if it is $\mathcal{S}_{\operatorname*{\odot}}^j$-independent for all $j\in[d]$, where 
 $\mathcal{S}_{\operatorname*{\odot}}^j$ is the spreadability system for the $\mathbb{C}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi^j)$ constructed in Section \ref{exaspread}.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Suppose that $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}$ is $\odot$-independent.  This means that  the identity  
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S-indep}
  \varphi_\pi^j(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) = \varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)}^j(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)  
\end{equation}
holds for $\pi = \hat 1_n$, any $j \in[d]$,  any tuple $(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)\in I^n$ and  any tuple of random variables $(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)$
  with $X_k\in  \mathcal{A}_{i_k}$, cf.\ \eqref{eq:univ_calculation}.   The goal is to verify \eqref{eq:S-indep} for any ordered set partition $\pi =(P_1,P_2,\dots, P_p)\in\mathcal{OP}_n$. 
  
  Let us denote $\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n) = (Q_1,Q_2,\dots, Q_q)$. Then $\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n) = (P_1 \cap Q_1, P_1 \cap Q_2, \dots, P_1 \cap  Q_q, P_2\cap Q_1, \dots, P_p \cap Q_q)$.  The RHS of \eqref{eq:S-indep} is exactly the value $\varphi^j(X_1X_2 \cdots X_n)$ when 
  \[
  (\{X_i\}_{i\in P_1\cap Q_1}, \{X_i\}_{i\in P_1 \cap Q_2}, \dots, \{X_i\}_{i\in P_1 \cap Q_q}, \{X_i\}_{i\in P_2 \cap Q_1}, \{X_i\}_{i\in P_2 \cap Q_2}, \dots)
  \]
  is assumed to be $\odot$-independent. The associativity of $\odot$ allows us to compute the RHS of \eqref{eq:S-indep} in the following two steps:    
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\alph*)]
\item\label{stepa} First compute $\varphi^j(X_1X_2 \cdots X_n)$ assuming that $(\{X_i\}_{i\in P_1}, \{X_i\}_{i\in P_2}, \dots, \{X_i\}_{i\in P_p})$ is $\odot$-independent. The result is exactly the RHS of \eqref{eq:univ_calculation}.   
\item\label{stepb} Then compute each factor $\varphi^{f(S)}(X_{S})$ by additionally assuming that 
\[
(\{X_i\}_{i\in S\cap Q_1}, \{X_i\}_{i\in S\cap Q_2}, \dots, \{X_i\}_{i\in S\cap Q_q})\] 
is $\odot$-independent.  
  \end{enumerate}
  This is exactly how the LHS of \eqref{eq:S-indep} is computed, so that \eqref{eq:S-indep} holds as desired.  
  
Conversely,  suppose that  $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}$ is  $\mathcal{S}_{\operatorname*{\odot}}^j$-independent for all $j\in[d]$. Formula \eqref{eq:S-indep} for  $\pi = \hat1_n$ is exactly the desired independence relation \eqref{eq:univ_calculation}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- exa-2: body_md -->
\label{exa:nonassociative0}
Let $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ be a $\mathbb{C}$-ncps and let $\mathcal{U}:= \sqcup_{i=1}^\infty \mathcal{A}$ be the coproduct in the category of algebras (see \eqref{eq:coproduct}) and $\iota^{(i)} \colon \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{U}$ be the natural embedding as $i^{\rm th}$ component. We define a linear functional $\tilde{\varphi}$ on $\mathcal{U}$ by, for each $X_1, X_2 , \dots, X_n \in \mathcal{A} $ and $i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $i_j \ne i_{j+1}$ for all $j =1,2,\dots, n-1$, setting 
\[
\tilde{\varphi}(X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots  X_n^{(i_n)}) 
= 
\begin{cases} 
\varphi(X_1) & \text{~if $n=1$}, \\ 
\varphi(X_1) \varphi(X_2) &  \text{~if $n =2$}, \\
0& \text{~if $n\ge3$}. 
\end{cases}
\]
Then we get an exchangeability system $(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i \in \mathbb{N}})$ for $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ with calculation rule.


For  $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ and $X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n \in \mathcal{A}$ it is easy to see that  
 \begin{equation} \label{eq:phi_pi}
      \varphi_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) =   
      \begin{cases} 
      \varphi_{(\pi)}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) & \text{~if~$\pi \in \mathcal{I}_n$ with $|\pi|\le2$,} \\ 
0 & \text{~otherwise}. 
      \end{cases}
    \end{equation} 
Suppose that subalgebras $\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{A}$ are $\mathcal{E}$-independent.  Then for $X \in \mathcal{B}_1$ and $Y \in \mathcal{B}_2$ we have 
$$
\varphi_{\pi}(X, Y)  = \varphi_{\pi \wedge \bar\kappa(1,2)}(X,Y)  
$$  
and the case $\pi =\hat1_2$ yields $\varphi(X Y) = \varphi(X) \varphi(Y)$. 
Moreover, independence implies 
$$
\varphi_{\pi}(X, Y, X)  = \varphi_{\pi \wedge \bar\kappa(1,2,1)}(X,Y,X). 
$$
On the other hand,
we infer from \eqref{eq:phi_pi} that
for $\pi = \{\{1,2\}, \{3\}\}$ the left hand side equals $\varphi(X Y) \varphi(X)
=\varphi(X)^2\varphi(Y)$, while the RHS equals zero.
This is only possible if either $\varphi \rfloor_{\mathcal{B}_1}=0$ or
$\varphi\rfloor_{\mathcal{B}_2}=0$ holds,
so that only the trivial examples satisfy $\mathcal{E}$-independence. However, nontrivial subalgebras $\{\mathcal{C}_1, \mathcal{C}_2\}$ satisfying condition \eqref{eq:weaker} exist because \eqref{eq:weaker} simply reads: if $X_j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_j}$ then for $\pi := \bar \kappa (i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n)$
 \begin{equation} \label{eq:phi_pi2}
      \varphi(X_1X_2\cdots X_n) =   
      \begin{cases} 
      \varphi_{(\pi)}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) & \text{~if~$\pi \in \mathcal{I}_n$ with $|\pi|\le2$,} \\ 
0 & \text{~otherwise}. 
      \end{cases}
    \end{equation} 
 For example we can start from any $\mathbb{C}$-ncps $(\mathcal{C}_i,\varphi_i), i=1,2$ and then construct $\varphi$ on $\mathcal{A} := \mathcal{C}_1 \sqcup \mathcal{C}_2$ so that  \eqref{eq:phi_pi2} holds.
<!-- end exa-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:exch:cumulants}
Let $\mathcal{E}=(\mathcal{U},\tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ be an
exchangeability system for a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$.  Cumulants are functionals satisfying the
the following requirements.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(E\arabic*)] 
 \item\label{it:Ecumulants:multi}
  \emph{Multilinearity}: Cumulants are multilinear functionals $K_\pi\colon \mathcal{A}^n\to\mathcal{B}$, indexed
  by set partitions $\pi\in\mathcal{P}_n$,   $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
   \item \emph{Universality}:
  There are universal coefficients $c(\sigma,\pi) \in \mathbb{C}$ such that
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:phipi=Kpi+sum}
  \varphi_\pi = K_\pi + \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n\\ \sigma<\pi}} c(\sigma,\pi) K_\sigma.
  \end{equation}

 \item\label{it:Ecumulants:vanish}  
  \emph{Vanishing of mixed cumulants}:
  given  a family $(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)\in\mathcal{A}^n$ and
  a partition $\pi\in\mathcal{P}_n$,
  such that some block of $P\in\pi$ can be partitioned
  $P=P' \dot\cup P''$ nontrivially in such a way that
  $\{X_i\mid i\in P'\}$ and   $\{X_i\mid i\in P''\}$ are $\mathcal{E}$-independent,
  then
  $$
  K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)=0
  .
  $$
  Equivalently, if $\rho\in\mathcal{P}_n$  partitions the family $(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)$
  into
  mutually $\mathcal{E}$-independent subfamilies,
  then $K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)=0$ unless $\pi\leq\rho$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\ 
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item \emph{Additivity}.
    As a consequence of
    \ref{it:Ecumulants:multi}
    and
    \ref{it:Ecumulants:vanish}
    cumulants of sums of independent random variables are additive:
    Denote by $K_n$ the cumulant functional $K_{\hat{1}_n}$, then
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:exch:additivity}
    K_n(X_1+Y_1,X_2+Y_2,\dots,X_n+Y_n) =
    K_n(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) +K_n(Y_1,Y_2,\dots,Y_n)
    .
    \end{equation}


   \item
    The system of equations \eqref{eq:phipi=Kpi+sum} is in triangular form and
    can be solved recursively and transformed into the equivalent system
    \begin{equation*}
K_\pi = \varphi_\pi  + \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n\\ \sigma<\pi}} \tilde{c}(\sigma,\pi) \varphi_\sigma
    \end{equation*}
    where the matrix $\tilde{c}(\sigma,\pi)$ is inverse to $c(\sigma,\pi)$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- defi-7: body_md -->
\label{def:dot}
 Let $(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i \geq 1})$ be a spreadability system for a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item  \label{eq:deltaAX} 
 Given a noncommutative random variable $X \in \mathcal{A}$ 
 and a finite subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ we define
 \begin{equation*} 
   \delta_A(X)=\sum_{i\in A} X^{(i)}   
 \end{equation*}
i.e., the sum of i.i.d.\ copies of $X$.
In the case $A=[N]$ we will also write $\delta_N(X)$ and frequently
abbreviate it using Rota's \emph{dot operation} 
$$
N.X:=X^{(1)} + X^{(2)} + \cdots + X^{(N)}
$$ 
whenever it is convenient.

\item We extend the partitioned functionals $\varphi_\pi$ to $\bigcup \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A})$ by setting
 \begin{equation}
   \label{eq:phipixjij}
 \varphi_{\pi}(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)}, \ldots,X_n^{(i_n)}):=\varphi_{\pi \curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n),    
 \end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}
     \label{eq:phipi(NX)}
 \varphi_\pi(N_1.X_1,N_2.X_2,\ldots,N_n.X_n):=
\sum_{i_1=1}^{N_1} 
\sum_{i_2=1}^{N_2} 
\dots
\sum_{i_n=1}^{N_n} 
 \varphi_{\pi}(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)}, \ldots,X_n^{(i_n)}). 
\end{equation}



\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-7 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
Note that \eqref{eq:phipixjij} is actually an abuse of notation,
  because $\varphi_\pi$ is defined for elements of $\mathcal{A}$ only 
  (see~\eqref{eq:phipi});
  here we pretend that 
  $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i=1}^\infty, \tilde{\varphi})$
  can be interpreted as a spreadability system for the algebra
  $\mathcal{A}^{(1,2,\dots,N)}$  generated by the images
  $\mathcal{A}^{(1)},\mathcal{A}^{(2)},\dots,\mathcal{A}^{(N)}$.
  This is true in the case of universal product construction in \eqref{eq:spreadability_universal_product} 
  but needs justification otherwise;
  yet \eqref{eq:phipixjij} is well-defined
  and convenient to keep notation manageable.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- defi-8: body_md -->
\label{def:spreadableK2}
  Let $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$ be a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps and $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U},\tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ a
  spreadability system for $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$.
  \emph{Cumulants} are multilinear functionals $K_\pi$ indexed
  by ordered set partitions $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$,
  which satisfy the following axioms. 



\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(S\arabic*)] 
 \item\label{S1}
\emph{Multilinearity}: Cumulants are multilinear functionals $K_\pi\colon \mathcal{A}^n\to\mathcal{B}$, indexed
  by ordered set partitions $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$,   $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
 \item\label{S2}
\emph{Universality}:
  There are universal coefficients $c(\sigma,\pi) \in \mathbb{C}$ such that
  for every $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$
  \begin{equation*}
\varphi_\pi = K_\pi + \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{OP}_n\\ \sigma<\pi}} c(\sigma,\pi) K_\sigma
  \end{equation*}
  or, equivalently,
  there are universal coefficients $\tilde{c}(\sigma,\pi) \in \mathbb{C}$ such that
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:SKpi=phipi+sum}
      K_\pi = \varphi_\pi  + \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{OP}_n\\ \sigma<\pi}} \tilde{c}(\sigma,\pi) \varphi_\sigma. 
    \end{equation}

   \item\label{S3}
\emph{Extensivity}:
  given  a family $(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)\in\mathcal{A}^n$ and
  an ordered partition $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$,
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:extensivity}
    K_{\pi}(N.X_1,N.X_2,\ldots,N.X_n) =N^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}K_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n), 
  \end{equation}
  where
  the  extension of $K_\pi$ to arguments from $\bigcup \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A})$ is defined via formula
  \eqref{eq:phipi(NX)}
  and
  \eqref{eq:SKpi=phipi+sum}
  as
\begin{align*}
K_\pi(X_1^{(i_1)},X_2^{(i_2)},\ldots,X_n^{(i_n)})
&:=  \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{OP}_n\\\sigma \leq \pi}}
    \tilde{c}(\sigma,\pi)\,\varphi_{\sigma}(X_1^{(i_1)},X_2^{(i_2)},\ldots,X_n^{(i_n)}) \\
&= \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{OP}_n\\\sigma \leq \pi}}
    \tilde{c}(\sigma,\pi)\,\varphi_{\sigma\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)
\intertext{and thus  }
K_\pi(N_1.X_1,N_2.X_2,\ldots,N_n.X_n)&:=  \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{OP}_n\\\sigma \leq \pi}}
     \tilde{c}(\sigma,\pi)\,\varphi_{\sigma}(N_1.X_1,N_2.X_2,\ldots,N_n.X_n),
\end{align*}
where the diagonal coefficients are $\tilde{c}(\pi,\pi)=1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-8 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:unique}
  Cumulants are uniquely determined by axioms \ref{S1}--\ref{S3} from
  Definition~\ref{def:spreadableK2}.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Assume that there are two sets of cumulants $K_\pi$ and $K'_\pi$ satisfying
  axioms \ref{S1}--\ref{S3} with universal coefficients $c(\sigma,\pi)$ and
  $c'(\sigma,\pi)$, respectively. Then the axioms imply that
      \begin{multline*}
        \varphi_{\pi}(N.X_1,N.X_2,\ldots,N.X_n)
        \\
      \begin{aligned}[t]
      &= N^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}K_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) + \sum_{\sigma < \pi} N^{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert}K_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,c(\sigma,\pi)  \\
      &= N^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}K'_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) + \sum_{\sigma < \pi} N^{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert}K'_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,c'(\sigma,\pi)
      \end{aligned}
      \end{multline*}
  for any $N\in\mathbb{N}$
  and the coefficients of the leading term $N^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}$ must coincide.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:quasimeetshift}
  Let $\pi\in \mathcal{OP}_n$ be an ordered set partition.
  Fix a block $P$ of $\pi$ and a number $m\in\mathbb{N}$
  and let $(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)$,  $(i'_1,i'_2,\dots,i'_n)$ be $n$-tuples
  such that
  $$
  i'_k=
  \begin{cases}
    i_k + m & \text{if $k\in P$}\\
    i_k     & \text{if $k\not\in P$}
  \end{cases}
  $$
  Then
  $\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)
  = \pi\curlywedge \kappa(i'_1,i'_2,\dots,i'_n)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
Note that without performing the quasi-meet operation in the lemma above
  the kernel partitions
  $\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)$ 
  and $\kappa(i'_1,i'_2,\dots,i'_n)$ 
  may well be nontrivial permutations of each other or even 
  $\bar\kappa(i_1',i_2',\dots,i_n')\ne\bar\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)$.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:iidsum}  
  For any ordered set partitions $\rho \le \pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ and numbers
  $N_1,N_2,\ldots\in\mathbb{N}$ we have
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:iidsum0}
  \varphi_{\rho}(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,N_{\pi(2)}.X_2,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)
    = \sum_{\sigma \leq \rho}\varphi_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,\gamma_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\rho, \pi),
\end{equation}
  with $\gamma_{\underline{N}}(\sigma, \rho, \pi)$ as in Definition~\ref{app:def:factorials} and $\pi(i)$ as in Definition \ref{defi:OP}\ref{item:OP2}. 
Specializing to the case $\rho=\pi$ yields
 \begin{align}
    \label{eq:iidsum}
  \varphi_{\pi}(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,N_{\pi(2)}.X_2,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)
    = \sum_{\sigma \leq \pi}\varphi_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,\beta_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\pi)
\end{align}
and this is a polynomial in $N_1,\dots, N_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}$ without constant term.
Furthermore, specializing to the case $N:=N_1 = N_2 = \cdots$ entails 
  $$
  \varphi_{\pi}(N.X_1,N.X_2,\ldots,N.X_n)
    = \sum_{\sigma \leq \pi}\varphi_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,\beta_N(\sigma,\pi),
  $$
 which is a polynomial in $N$ consisting of monomials of degree at least $\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We begin with \eqref{eq:iidsum} and then verify the general case \eqref{eq:iidsum0}.  The proof boils down to the enumeration of the set
  \[
 S_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\pi):= \{(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)\in [N_{\pi(1)}] \times [N_{\pi(2)}] \times \cdots \times [N_{\pi(n)}]: \pi \curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)=\sigma
  \}. 
  \]
  Pick an arbitrary block
  $P_i=\{p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_k\}$ of $\pi = (P_1,P_2,\dots)$.  There are $\binom{N_i}{\#(\sigma\rfloor_{P_i})}$ possible
  ways to choose a tuple $(i_{p_1},i_{p_2}, \ldots, i_{p_k})$ such that
  $\kappa(i_{p_1},i_{p_2}, \ldots, i_{p_k})$ 
  defines the partition $\sigma\rfloor_{P_i}$:
  for each block of $\sigma\rfloor_{P_i}$ we have to choose
  a distinct label from $[N_i]$ respecting the order prescribed by the
  labels of the blocks of $\sigma\rfloor_{P_i}$.
  That is, we have to choose a subset of $[N_i]$ of cardinality 
  $\#(\sigma\rfloor_{P_i})$.
  This can be done for every block of $\pi$ independently
  and thus
  \begin{equation}\label{eq cardinality} 
  \# S_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\pi)=\prod_{i =1}^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert} \binom{N_i}{\#(\sigma\rfloor_{P_i})}=\beta_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\pi).
  \end{equation}
   If $N_i <\#(\sigma\rfloor_{P_i})$ for some $i$, then $\pi \curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)$ can never be equal to $\sigma$, and so 
    the cardinality of $ S_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\pi)$ is 0, in accordance
    with the generally adopted convention that the generalized
    binomial coefficient $\binom{N}{k}$ is zero when $N<k$. 
    
    The general formula \eqref{eq:iidsum0} requires the enumeration of the set
    \[
 S_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\rho,\pi) = \{(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)\in [N_{\pi(1)}] \times [N_{\pi(2)}] \times \cdots \times [N_{\pi(n)}]: \rho \curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)=\sigma
  \}.   
  \]
This is similar to $S_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\rho)$; the difference is that the blocks of $\rho$ contained in a block $P_i \in \pi$ are endowed with the common number $N_i$. This results in the product formula
\[
\# S_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\rho,\pi) = \prod_{i=1}^p  S_{N_i}(\sigma \rfloor_{P_i},\rho \rfloor_{P_i}),  
\]
which equals $\gamma_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\rho,\pi)$ from Remark \ref{rem:beta_gamma}\ref{item:beta_gamma}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- defi-9: body_md -->
\label{def:cumulants} 
  Given an ordered set partition $\pi=(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_k) \in \mathcal{OP}_n$
  with $k$ blocks, 
  we define the \emph{partitioned cumulant} $K_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)$ to be the coefficient of
$N_1N_2\dotsm N_k$ in the polynomial
    \eqref{eq:iidsum}.
<!-- end defi-9 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:mc} For any $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$, we have 
  \begin{align}
  K_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)  &= \sum_{\sigma \leq \pi}  \varphi_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,  \widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\pi),    \label{eq:Kpi=sumphisi}  \\  
  \varphi_{\pi}(X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n) &= \sum_{\sigma \leq \pi} K_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,\widetilde{\zeta}(\sigma,\pi)  \label{eq:phipi=sumKsi}    
  \end{align}
 with $ \widetilde{\mu}, \widetilde{\zeta}$ as in Definition~\ref{app:def:factorials}.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For $0<k<N$, 
there is no constant term in $\binom{N}{k}= \frac{N(N-1)\cdots (N-k+1)}{k!}$ 
(regarded as a polynomial in $N$), and the coefficient of its linear term is 
$\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k+1)}{k!} = \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k}$. 
Therefore the coefficient of $N_1 \cdots N_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}$ in $\beta_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\pi)=\prod_{i=1}^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}\binom{N_i}{\#(\sigma\rfloor_{P_i})}$ is equal to $\frac{(-1)^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert-\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert}}{[\sigma:\pi]}$. Note that $\sum_{P\in\pi}\#(\sigma\rfloor_P)=\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert$. 
Comparing with  \eqref{eq:mutilde} the claimed formula \eqref{eq:Kpi=sumphisi}  follows.
The same argument holds true if we look at the monomial $N^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}$ 
when $N_1 =N_2= \cdots =N$.   


The inverse formula \eqref{eq:phipi=sumKsi} expressing moments in terms of
cumulants
is an immediate consequence of the fact that the modified M\"{o}bius function
$\widetilde{\mu}$
is the inverse of the modified zeta function $\widetilde{\zeta}$
(Corollary~\ref{app:cor:inversion}).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
The cumulants defined in Definition~\ref{def:cumulants} verify the axioms \emph{\ref{S1}--\ref{S3}} from
  Definition~\ref{def:spreadableK2}.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- defi-10: body_md -->
For $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$ and $M_i, N_i \in \mathbb{N}, i=1,2,\dots,n$, we define
 \begin{multline*}
\varphi_\pi(M_1.(N_1.X_1),M_2.(N_2.X_2), \ldots,M_n.(N_n.X_n)) \\
:= \sum_{(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n) \in[M_1] \times [M_2] \times \cdots \times [M_n]} \varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)}(N_1.X_1, N_2.X_2,\ldots,N_n.X_n). 
  \end{multline*}
<!-- end defi-10 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
We would like to alert the reader that the formal definition of the expectation
 \[
 \varphi_\pi(M_1.(N_1.X_1),M_2.(N_2.X_2),\ldots,M_n.(N_n.X_n))
 \] 
is not necessarily related
to ``$M.(N.X)$'' (which formally would represent the element
$
(N.X)^{(1)}+(N.X)^{(2)}+\cdots +(N.X)^{(M)}
,
$
i.e., 
``the sum of i.i.d.\ copies of $N.X$'')
as an element of an enlarged space,
obtained, e.g., by iterating a product construction.
Yet we will show below that the vector
$(M_{\pi(1)}N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,\ldots, M_{\pi(n)}N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)$ and
the virtual vector ``$(M_{\pi(1)}.(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1),
\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}.(N_{\pi(n)}.X_n))$'' have the same distribution with respect to $\varphi_\pi$.
This property implies extensivity of cumulants, see Proposition~\ref{ad} below. 
It is a consequence of the associativity of the corresponding universal product in the case of classical, free, monotone and Boolean independence \cite{HS11b}.
For general spreadability systems it holds on a formal level
(Lemma~\ref{prop5}), even when it comes from a nonassociative
universal product, like the example of V-monotone independence from 
Section~\ref{sssec:vmonotone}.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{prop5} Let $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$, $X_i \in \mathcal{A}$ and $M_i,N_i \in \mathbb{N}, i=1,2,\dots, \left\lvert \pi \right\rvert$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]

\item\label{Polynomial} The value
 $\varphi_\pi(M_{\pi(1)}.(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1),\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}.(N_{\pi(n)}.X_n))$ is
 a polynomial in the variables $M_i,N_i, i=1,2,\dots, \left\lvert \pi \right\rvert$,  and 
$K_\pi(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)$ is the coefficient of $M_1 \cdots M_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}$. 

\item \label{Associative-like} The dot operation gives rise to an action of the
 multiplicative semigroup $\mathbb{N}^\infty$
 \begin{multline*}
   \varphi_\pi(M_{\pi(1)}N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)
   \\
   = \varphi_\pi(M_{\pi(1)}.(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1),\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}.(N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)). 
 \end{multline*}


\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
\ref{Polynomial}\,\, Let $\underline{M}:=(M_1,\dots, M_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert},0,0,\dots)\in \mathbb{N}^\infty$ and similarly $\underline{N} \in \mathbb{N}^\infty$. 
  Then the following expansion holds:
  \begin{multline}\label{eq20}
     \varphi_\pi(M_{\pi(1)}.(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1),\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}.(N_{\pi(n)}.X_n))\\
    \begin{aligned}
      &= \sum_{(i_1,\dots, i_n) \in [M_{\pi(1)}]\times \cdots \times [M_{\pi(n)}]} \varphi_{\pi \curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)}(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n) \\ 
      &=\sum_{\sigma \leq \pi} \sum_{\substack{(i_1,\dots, i_n) \in [M_{\pi(1)}]\times \cdots \times [M_{\pi(n)}],\\ \pi \curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)=\sigma}} \varphi_{\sigma}(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n) \\
      &=  \sum_{\sigma \leq \pi} \varphi_{\sigma}(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n) \,\beta_{\underline{M}}(\sigma,\pi), 
    \end{aligned}
    \end{multline}
 where we used the identity \eqref{eq cardinality}. Hence $\varphi_\pi(M_{\pi(1)}.(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1),\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}.(N_{\pi(n)}.X_n))$ is a polynomial in $M_i,N_i, i=1,2,\dots, \left\lvert \pi \right\rvert$, 
  and from the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:mc} 
we infer that the coefficient of $M_1\cdots M_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}$ is equal to $K_\pi(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent
\ref{Associative-like}\,\, We proceed with the computation of \eqref{eq20}:
\begin{multline*}
     \varphi_\pi(M_{\pi(1)}.(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1),M_{\pi(2)}.(N_{\pi(2)}.X_2),\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}.(N_{\pi(n)}.X_n))\\
    \begin{aligned}
         &= \sum_{\rho \leq \pi} 
             \varphi_{\rho}(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,N_{\pi(2)}.X_2,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)
             \,\beta_{\underline{M}}(\rho,\pi) \\
          &= \sum_{\rho \leq \pi} 
             \sum_{\sigma \le \rho }
              \varphi_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2, \ldots,X_n) 
              \, \gamma_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\rho,\pi)
              \, \beta_{\underline{M}}(\rho,\pi)\\ 
          &= \sum_{\sigma\leq \pi}
             \varphi_{\sigma}(X_1, X_2,\ldots,X_n)
             \biggl(  \sum_{\substack{\rho\in\mathcal{OP}_n  \\ \sigma \leq \rho \leq \pi}}
               \gamma_{\underline{N}}(\sigma,\rho,\pi)
               \, \beta_{\underline{M}}(\rho,\pi) 
             \biggr)\\ 
          &= \sum_{\sigma \leq \pi} \varphi_\sigma(X_1, X_2,\ldots,X_n) (\gamma_{\underline{N}} \otriangle \beta_{\underline{M}}) (\sigma,\pi)\\
          &= \sum_{ \sigma \leq \pi} \varphi_\sigma(X_1, X_2,\ldots,X_n) \,\beta_{\underline{M} \circ \underline{N}}(\sigma,\pi) \\
          &= \varphi_{\pi}(M_{\pi(1)}N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,M_{\pi(2)}N_{\pi(2)}.X_2,\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}N_{\pi(n)}.X_n), 
    \end{aligned}
\end{multline*}
    where  \eqref{eq:iidsum0} was used in the second equality and Corollary~\ref{app:cor:inversion} was used in the next to last line.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{ad}
  The cumulants from 
 Definition~\ref{def:cumulants}  satisfy extensivity \eqref{eq:extensivity} and more generally, 
  \begin{equation*}
  K_{\pi}(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1,N_{\pi(2)}.X_2,\ldots,N_{\pi(n)}.X_n) =N_1N_2 \cdots N_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}K_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n). 
  \end{equation*}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By definition, $\varphi_\pi$ applied to the same arguments has the expansion
  \begin{multline*}
  \varphi_{\pi}(M_{\pi(1)}N_{\pi(1)}.X_1, M_{\pi(2)}N_{\pi(2)}.X_2,\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}N_{\pi(n)}.X_n)
\\
  =\Biggl(
      \prod_{i=1}^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}M_i N_i
      \Biggr)
      K_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) + (\text{sum of monomials in $M_i N_i$ of higher degrees}). 
  \end{multline*}
    On the other hand, from Lemma~\ref{prop5}\ref{Polynomial} we infer
    \begin{multline*}
      \varphi_{\pi}(M_{\pi(1)}.(N_{\pi(1)}.X_1),
      M_{\pi(2)}.(N_{\pi(2)}.X_2),\ldots,M_{\pi(n)}.(N_{\pi(n)}.X_n))
      \\
      = M_1 M_2 \cdots M_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert} K_{\pi}(N.X_1,N.X_2,\ldots,N.X_n)
      \\
+ (\text{sum of monomials in $M_i$ of higher degree}). 
    \end{multline*}
We have thus computed the expectation in two ways and
it follows from Lemma~\ref{prop5}\ref{Associative-like} that the coefficients of $M_1 \cdots M_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}$  coincide.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{inv:permutation}
  If a spreadability system $\mathcal{S}$ satisfies exchangeability, 
  then both the partitioned expectations and cumulants are invariant under permutations of the
  blocks.
  More precisely,
  for any partition $\pi=(P_1,P_2, \dots,P_k) \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ and permutation $h \in \mathfrak{S}_k$,
  $\varphi_\pi = \varphi_{h(\pi)}$ and
  $K_\pi = K_{h(\pi)}$,   where $h(\pi)=(P_{h(1)}, P_{h(2)}, \dots,P_{h(k)})$,
  Thus $\varphi_\pi$ and $K_\pi$ are completely determined by the underlying (unordered) set partition $\bar{\pi}$.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Invariance of $\varphi_\pi$ under permutations of the blocks of $\pi$ is an immediate consequence of
   exchangeability and this invariance extends to the extension  \eqref{eq:phipixjij}.
   Indeed let $\pi=(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_k)\in\mathcal{OP}_n$ and  $i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n \in \mathbb{N}$,
   then for any $h \in \mathfrak{S}_k$ there exists a permutation $g \in \mathfrak{S}_\infty$
   such that
   $h(\pi)\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n) = g(\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n) )$. Therefore, 
\begin{align*}
\varphi_{h(\pi)}(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)},\dots, X_n^{(i_n)}) &= \varphi_{h(\pi)\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) \\
&= \varphi_{g(\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n))}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)  \\
&= \varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) \\
&=\varphi_{\pi}(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)},\dots, X_n^{(i_n)}). 
\end{align*}
Consequently also $\varphi_\pi(N.X_1,N.X_2,\dots,N.X_n) =
\varphi_{h(\pi)}(N.X_1,N.X_2,\dots,N.X_n)$ and,
by definition,  $K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = K_{h(\pi)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:mc}
  If a spreadability system $\mathcal{S}$ satisfies exchangeability
  then  for $\pi \in \mathcal{P}_n$  we simply write $K_\pi$ for the partitioned
  cumulant functional uniquely determined in Proposition~\ref{inv:permutation}.
  Then for any $\pi \in \mathcal{P}_n$, we have 
  \begin{align}
  K_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)  &= \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{P}_n \\ \sigma \leq \pi}}  \varphi_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,  \mu_{\mathcal{P}}(\sigma,\pi),    \label{eq:Kpi=sumphisi2}  \\  
  \varphi_{\pi}(X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n) &= \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{P}_n \\ \sigma \leq \pi}} K_{\sigma}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n), \label{eq:phipi=sumKsi2}    
  \end{align}
where $\mu_{\mathcal{P}}$ is the M\"obius function on the posets $\mathcal{P}_n, n\in \mathbb{N}$, see \eqref{app:eq:SPmoebius}.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- exa-3: body_md -->
We will write the ordered kernel set partition $\kappa(i_1,\dots, i_n)$
  simply as the multiset permutation $i_1i_2\dots i_n$. For example,
  $211=(\{2,3\},\{1\})$.  
  Examples of Theorem~\ref{thm:mc} are given by 
\begin{align*}
K_1(X) &= \varphi_1(X), \\
K_{11}(X, Y) &= \varphi_{11}(X,Y) - \frac{1}{2}(\varphi_{12}(X,Y) + \varphi_{21}(X,Y)), \\
K_{12}(X,Y) &= \varphi_{12}(X,Y), \\
K_{21}(X,Y) &= \varphi_{21}(X,Y), \\
K_{111} &= \varphi_{111} - \frac{1}{2}(\varphi_{112}+\varphi_{121}+\varphi_{122}+\varphi_{211}+\varphi_{212}+\varphi_{221}) \\ \notag
&\qquad+\frac{1}{3}(\varphi_{123}+\varphi_{132}+\varphi_{213}+\varphi_{231}+\varphi_{312}+\varphi_{321}), \\
K_{112} &= \varphi_{112} - \frac{1}{2}(\varphi_{123}+\varphi_{213}), 
\end{align*}
where for the sake of compactness the arguments $(X,Y,Z)$ are omitted 
in the last two formulas.
<!-- end exa-3 -->
<!-- exa-4: body_md -->
Examples of Theorem~\ref{thm:mc} are given by 
\begin{align*}
\varphi_1(X) &= K_1(X), \\
\varphi_{11}(X, Y) &= K_{11}(X,Y) + \frac{1}{2!}(K_{12}(X,Y) + K_{21}(X,Y)), \\
\varphi_{12}(X,Y) &= K_{12}(X,Y), \\
\varphi_{21}(X,Y) &= K_{21}(X,Y), \\
\varphi_{111} &= K_{111} + \frac{1}{2!}(K_{112}+K_{121}+K_{122}+K_{211}+K_{212}+K_{221}) \\ \notag
&\qquad+\frac{1}{3!}(K_{123}+K_{132}+K_{213}+K_{231}+K_{312}+K_{321}), \\
\varphi_{112} &= K_{112} + \frac{1}{2!}(K_{123}+K_{213}), 
\end{align*}
where $(X,Y,Z)$ are omitted in the last two formulas for simplicity.
<!-- end exa-4 -->
<!-- defi-11: body_md -->
\label{def:multiplicative} 
  For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ the  $n$-linear maps on $\mathcal{A}$
$$
K_n:=K_{\hat{1}_n}, \qquad \varphi_n:=\varphi_{\hat{1}_n}
$$
are called the  $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ cumulant and expectation functional,
respectively.
The latter is simply
$$
\varphi_n(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)
=\varphi(X_1X_2  \cdots X_n)
$$
for $X_i \in \mathcal{A}$.
Following notation \eqref{eq:phipixjij},
we also write
$$
\varphi_n(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)}, \dots, X_n^{(i_n)})
=\tilde{\varphi}(X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots X_n^{(i_n)})
.
$$
We extend these functionals
multiplicatively to set partitions and 
ordered set partitions as follows.

  For set partitions $\pi\in\mathcal{P}_n$  we define multiplicative extensions
  $\varphi_{(\pi)}$ of $(\varphi_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $K_{(\pi)}$ of $(K_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ 
  by setting
  \begin{align*}
    &\varphi_{(\pi)}(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots, Y_n) :=\prod_{P\in \pi} \varphi_{\left\lvert P \right\rvert}(Y_P)   \qquad \text{and} \qquad  K_{(\pi)}(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots, Y_n) :=\prod_{P\in \pi} K_{\left\lvert P \right\rvert}(Y_P)\\
   &\qquad\qquad \text{for} \quad Y_1,Y_2,\dots, Y_n\in \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A}) \quad \text{or} \quad Y_1, Y_2,\dots, Y_n \in \mathcal{A},
  \end{align*}
  where we use notation \eqref{notation:linear}  for multilinear functionals. 
We also define $\varphi_{(\pi)}:=\varphi_{(\bar{\pi})}$ and $K_{(\pi)}:=K_{(\bar{\pi})}$ for ordered set partitions $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$.
<!-- end defi-11 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:factorization}
 Let $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$ be an ordered set partition.  
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item\label{item:factorization1}  Let $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde \varphi, (\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ be a spreadability system for some $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$. Assume that there exists a family of complex numbers 
$
\{s(\sigma; \pi): \sigma \in \mathcal{P}_n, \sigma \le \bar\pi\}
$ 
such that 
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:lem:factorization1} 
\varphi_\pi(Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_n) =   \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{P}_n\\ \sigma \le \bar\pi }} s(\sigma; \pi) \varphi_{(\sigma)}(Y_1,Y_2,\dots, Y_n)
  \end{equation}
    holds for any tuple of random variables $Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_n \in  \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A})$. 
    Then 
    \begin{equation*}
    K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)=  s(\bar\pi;\pi) K_{(\pi)}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)
    \end{equation*}
    for any tuple $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n \in \mathcal{A}$.   \item\label{item:factorization2}
    Let $(\mathcal{U}, \tilde \varphi, (\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ be a spreadability
    system for some $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$.
    Assume that there exist coefficients
    $
    \{t(\rho; \pi): \rho \in \mathcal{OP}_n, \bar \sigma < \bar \pi\}
    $ 
    such that 
   \begin{equation*}
\varphi_\pi(Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_n) =  \sum_{\substack{\rho \in \mathcal{OP}_n\\ \bar \rho < \bar \pi }} t(\rho; \pi) \varphi_{\rho}(Y_1,Y_2,\dots, Y_n)
  \end{equation*}
   holds for any tuple of random variables $Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_n \in
   \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A})$.
   Then the cumulant $K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)=0$  for any tuple $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n \in \mathcal{A}$.  
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
Suppose the expansion \eqref{eq:lem:factorization1}
  holds for all ordered set partitions $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$, then $\mathcal{S}$ is a
  spreadability system with calculation rule \eqref{eq:calculation_rule} (e.g.\
  take $Y_1,Y_2,\dots, Y_n \in \iota^{(1)}(\mathcal{A})$).
  Now the expansion \eqref{eq:lem:factorization1} extends the calculation rule to the variables
  $Y_1,Y_2,\dots$ in $\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A})$.
  Such an extension is not automatic; we give a counterexample in Example \ref{exa:nonassociative}.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
\ref{item:factorization1}  Choosing $Y_k = \iota^{(i_k)}(X_k)$ and taking the sum of  \eqref{eq:lem:factorization1} over all indices $i_1, i_2,\dots, i_n \in [N]$ we get formula \eqref{eq:lem:factorization1} for $Y_k = N. X_k$ as well. The desired conclusion is  an immediate consequence by comparing the coefficients of $N^{|\pi|}$ together with the definition of cumulants (Definition~\ref{def:cumulants}). 
The point is that, since the number of blocks of any $\sigma<\bar \pi$ is strictly larger than the number of blocks of $\pi$, the coefficient of $N^{|\pi|}$ vanishes in $\varphi_{(\sigma)}(N.X_1,N.X_2,\dots,N.X_n)$.    \ref{item:factorization2} is proven in a similar way.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop19}   \
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item\label{ten}
    Let $K^{\mathrm{T}}_\pi$ be the cumulants associated to the tensor spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{T}}$. Then 
    \begin{equation*}
    K^{\mathrm{T}}_\pi=K^{\mathrm{T}}_{(\pi)},\qquad \pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n. 
    \end{equation*}


   \item\label{fre}
    Let $K^{\mathrm{F}}_\pi$ be the cumulants associated to the free spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{F}}$. Then  
    \begin{equation*}
    K^{\mathrm{F}}_\pi=
    \begin{cases}
      0, &\pi \notin \mathcal{ONC}_n, \\
      K^{\mathrm{F}}_{(\pi)},& \pi \in \mathcal{ONC}_n
    \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    where by $\mathcal{ONC}_n$ we denote the set of ordered noncrossing partitions,
    see Definition~\ref{app:def:OSPclass}     \ref{app:def:ONC}.

   \item\label{boole} 
    Let $K^{\mathrm{T}}_\pi$ be the cumulants associated to the Boolean spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{B}}$. Then 
    \begin{equation*}
    K^{\mathrm{B}}_\pi=
    \begin{cases}
      0, &\pi \notin \mathcal{OI}_n, \\
      K^{\mathrm{B}}_{(\pi)},& \pi \in \mathcal{OI}_n
    \end{cases}
  \end{equation*}
    where by $\mathcal{OI}_n$ we denote the set of ordered interval partitions,    
    see Definition~\ref{app:def:OSPclass}     \ref{app:def:OI}.
   \item\label{it:mon}
   Let $K^{\mathrm{M}}_\pi$ be the cumulants associated to the monotone spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{M}}$. Then 
    \begin{equation*}
    K^{\mathrm{M}}_\pi=
    \begin{cases}
      0, &\pi \notin \mathcal{M}_n, \\
      K^{\mathrm{M}}_{(\pi)},& \pi \in \mathcal{M}_n
    \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    where by $\mathcal{M}_n$ we denote the set of monotone partitions,
    see Definition~\ref{app:def:OSPclass}     \ref{app:def:monopart}.
\end{enumerate}
These results combined with the general moment-cumulant formula (Theorem \ref{thm:mc}) reproduce the known formulas.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Items \ref{ten}, \ref{fre} and \ref{boole} satisfy exchangeability
  and are covered  in~\cite{L04} (note that our cumulants are invariant under the permutation of the blocks of $\pi$, see Proposition~\ref{inv:permutation});
  alternatively these cases follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:factorization} and the arguments below.

  We are left with case \ref{it:mon}.
  Let $u_{\rm M}(\sigma; \pi)$ be the universal coefficients from Axiom
  \ref{U6} for monotone independence
  (where $f \colon \sigma \to [1]$ is unique and hence omitted).  
  We can prove \eqref{eq:lem:factorization1} for $s(\sigma; \pi) :=  u_{\mathrm{M}}(\sigma; \pi)$
  using the technique from the proof of
  Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence_independences}.
  Indeed,
  associativity allows us to deduce the identity
  $$
  \varphi_{\pi}(X_1^{(i_1)},X_2^{(i_2)},\dots, X_n^{(i_n)})= \varphi_{\pi
    \curlywedge \kappa(i_1,\dots, i_n)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)
  $$
  following the two steps \ref{stepa} and \ref{stepb} there
  and the resulting value is exactly  the RHS of
  \eqref{eq:lem:factorization1} with $Y_k = X_k^{(i_k)}$. 
  It is known that $u_{\rm M}(\bar{\pi}; \pi)=1$ for $\pi \in \mathcal{M}_n$ and
  $u_{\rm M}(\bar{\pi}; \pi)=0$ for $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n \setminus \mathcal{M}_n$, see
  \cite[Prop.~3.2]{Muraki:2002:five} and the claimed formula follows.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
Other examples of noncrossing cumulants come from the c-free
  exchangeability systems of \cite{BLS96}, see \cite[Section~4.7]{L04}.
  Lemma~\ref{lem:factorization} \ref{item:factorization2} provides a new
  proof that crossing cumulants vanish.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop20} 
 Let $K^{\mathrm{CM}}_\pi$ be the $\pi$-cumulant associated to the c-monotone spreadability
 system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{CM}}$ defined in Section \ref{sssec:cmonotone} and
 $K^{{\mathrm{M}},\psi}_n$ the $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ monotone cumulant functional with
 respect to the linear map $\psi:\mathcal{A}\to \mathbb{C}$.
 Then
  \[
  \displaystyle 
  K^{\mathrm{CM}}_\pi(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)=
  \begin{cases}
    \displaystyle \prod_{P \in \mathrm{Outer}(\pi)}K^{\mathrm{CM}}_{\left\lvert P \right\rvert}(X_P) \prod_{P \in \mathrm{Inner}(\pi)}K^{{\mathrm{M}},\psi}_{\left\lvert P \right\rvert}(X_P),& \pi \in \mathcal{M}_n, 
    \\
    0, &\pi \notin \mathcal{M}_n 
  \end{cases}
  \]
 with $\mathrm{Outer}(\pi)$ and $\mathrm{Inner}(\pi)$ the sets of outer blocks of $\pi$ and inner blocks of $\pi$, respectively; see Definition \ref{app:def:partitions} \ref{item:app:def:partitions2}.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We use two spreadability systems: the c-monotone spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{CM}}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i=1}^\infty)$ for $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$ and the monotone spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{M}}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\psi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i=1}^\infty)$ for $(\mathcal{A},\psi)$. 
  The multiplicative extension $\varphi_{(\pi)}$ of $\varphi$ is now modified to
  \begin{align*}
 & \varphi_{(\pi), \psi}(Y_1, Y_2,\ldots, Y_n) 
  := \prod_{P \in \mathrm{Outer}(\pi)}\varphi_{\left\lvert P \right\rvert}(Y_P) \prod_{P \in \mathrm{Inner}(\pi)}\psi_{\left\lvert P \right\rvert}(Y_P) \\
    & \qquad \text{for} \quad \pi\in\mathcal{ONC}_n,  \quad Y_1,Y_2,\dots, Y_n\in \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A}) \quad \text{or} \quad Y_1, Y_2,\dots, Y_n \in \mathcal{A},
  \end{align*}
  which apparently coincides with $\varphi_{(\pi)}$ if $\varphi=\psi$. 
  By the definition of c-monotone spreadability system, there exist universal constants
  $u_{\mathrm{CM}}(\sigma, f; \pi) \in \mathbb{C}$ depending only on  $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n, \sigma \in\mathcal{P}_n$
  with $\bar\pi > \sigma$ and a ``2-coloring'' $f$ of the blocks of $\sigma$,
  i.e.\ a function $f\colon \sigma\to \{1,2\}$, such that   for any $Y_j\in \mathcal{A}$
\begin{multline*}
    \varphi_\pi(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_n)
    =
      \varphi_{(\pi), \psi}(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_n)
    \\
      +
\sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n,  \sigma <\bar{\pi} \\  f\colon\,
          \sigma\to \{1,2\} }}u_{\mathrm{CM}}(\sigma, f; \pi)
      \Bigl(\prod_{f(S)=1}\varphi_{\left\lvert S \right\rvert}(Y_S)\Bigr)
      \Bigl(\prod_{f(S)=2}\psi_{\left\lvert S \right\rvert}(Y_S)\Bigr)
\end{multline*}
if $\pi \in \mathcal{M}_n$ and
$$
\varphi_\pi(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_n)  =
\sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n,  \sigma <\bar{\pi} \\  f\colon\, \sigma\to     \{1,2\} }}
    u_{\mathrm{CM}}(\sigma, f; \pi)
    \Bigl(\prod_{f(S)=1}\varphi_{\left\lvert S \right\rvert}(Y_S)\Bigr)
    \Bigl(\prod_{f(S)=2}\psi_{\left\lvert S \right\rvert}(Y_S)\Bigr)
$$ if $\pi \notin \mathcal{M}_n$.
 Similar to the monotone case, thanks to associativity and
the arguments from the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence_independences}, 
this formula holds also for $Y_j \in  \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty
\iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A}), j\in[n]$. Then the arguments from Lemma~\ref{lem:factorization} and Proposition \ref{prop19} applies.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- exa-5: body_md -->
\label{exa:nonassociative}
Let $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ be a $\mathbb{C}$-ncps and let $\mathcal{U}:= \sqcup_{i=1}^\infty \mathcal{A}$ be the coproduct in the category of algebras (see \eqref{eq:coproduct}) and $\iota^{(i)} \colon \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{U}$ be the natural embedding as $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ component. We define a linear functional $\tilde{\varphi}$ on $\mathcal{U}$ by, for each $X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n \in \mathcal{A}$ and $i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $i_j \ne i_{j+1}$ for all $j =1,2,\dots, n-1$, setting 
\[
\tilde{\varphi}(X_1^{(i_1)} X_2^{(i_2)} \cdots X_n^{(i_n)}) 
= 
\begin{cases} 
0& \text{~if there are $k \ne \ell$ such that $i_k=i_\ell$}, \\
\prod_{i=1}^n \varphi(X_i) &  \text{~otherwise}.  
\end{cases}
\]
Then we get an exchangeability system $(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i \in \mathbb{N}})$ for $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$. 


For  $\pi \in \mathcal{P}_n$ and $X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n \in \mathcal{A}$ it is easy to see that  
 \begin{equation}
      \varphi_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) =   
      \begin{cases} \varphi_{(\pi)}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) & \text{~if~} \pi \in \mathcal{I}_n, \\
      0 & \text{~otherwise}
      \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
    holds for any tuple $X_i \in \mathcal{A}$; however this formula does not extend
    to mixed tuples $Y_i \in \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A})$. For example, if $\pi=\{\{1,3\},\{2\}\}$ then 
    \[
\varphi_\pi(X_1^{(1)}, X_2^{(2)}, X_3^{(3)}) = \varphi(X_1) \varphi(X_2) \varphi(X_3) = \varphi(X_1^{(1)}) \varphi(X_2^{(2)}) \varphi(X_3^{(3)}) 
\] 
but \[
\varphi_\pi(X_1^{(1)}, X_2^{(1)}, X_3^{(1)}) =0 \ne \varphi(X_1^{(1)}) \varphi(X_2^{(1)}) \varphi(X_3^{(1)}) 
\] 
in general. 


Next we shall compute some cumulants. Straightforward calculations yield
\begin{align*}
\varphi_{\hat{1}_1} (N. X_1) &= N \varphi(X_1), \\
\varphi_{\hat{1}_2}(N.X_1,N.X_2) &= N \varphi(X_1X_2) + N(N-1) \varphi(X_1) \varphi(X_2), \\
  \varphi_{\hat{1}_3}(N.X_1, N.X_2, N.X_3)
    &= \begin{multlined}[t]
      N \varphi(X_1 X_2 X_3) + N(N-1) \varphi(X_1 X_2) \varphi(X_3)
      \\
      +  N(N-1) \varphi(X_1) \varphi(X_2 X_3)
      \\
      + N(N-1) (N-2) \varphi(X_1)\varphi( X_2) \varphi(X_3),  
    \end{multlined}
\end{align*}
so that the coefficients of $N$ yield the cumulants  
\begin{align*}
K_1 (X_1) &= \varphi(X_1), \\
K_2(X_1,X_2) &=  \varphi(X_1X_2) - \varphi(X_1) \varphi(X_2), \\
K_3(X_1, X_2, X_3) &= \varphi(X_1 X_2 X_3) - \varphi(X_1 X_2) \varphi(X_3) - \varphi(X_1) \varphi(X_2 X_3) + 2 \varphi(X_1)\varphi( X_2) \varphi(X_3).   
\end{align*}
On the other hand, for $\pi = \{\{1,3\},\{2\}\}$ we have 
\begin{align*}
\varphi_{\pi}(N.X_1, N.X_2, N.X_3) 
  &= \sum_{\substack{ i_1,i_2,i_3 \\ i_1 = i_3}}     \sum_{i_1 = i_3}
      \varphi_{\pi}(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)}, X_3^{(i_3)})
    + \sum_{\substack{i_1,i_2,i_3 \\ i_1 \ne i_3}}
       \varphi_{\pi}(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)}, X_3^{(i_3)})  \\
  &= \sum_{\substack{i_1,i_2,i_3 \\ i_1 = i_3}}
  \underbrace{\varphi_{\pi}(X_1, X_2, X_3)}_{\text{$=0$}}
  + \sum_{\substack{i_1,i_2,i_3  \\ i_1 \ne i_3}}
     \varphi_{\hat{0}_3}(X_1, X_2, X_3) \\
&= 
N^2(N-1) \varphi(X_1)\varphi(X_2) \varphi(X_3), 
\end{align*}
so that 
\[
K_{\pi}(X_1, X_2, X_3) = - \varphi(X_1)\varphi(X_2) \varphi(X_3), 
\]
which does not vanish in general although the underlying set partition $\pi$ is not interval. This does not contradict Lemma~\ref{lem:factorization} 
because condition \eqref{eq:lem:factorization1} is not satisfied.
Indeed, the only possible identity would be
$\varphi_{\{13/2\}}(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3) = c \varphi_{\{1/2/3\}}(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)$
for every $Y_j\in\bigcup \iota^{(i)}(\mathcal{A})$.
However the combinations
$\varphi_{\{13/2\}}(X_1^{(1)},X_2^{(1)},X_3^{(1)}) =
\varphi_{\{13/2\}}(X_1,X_2,X_3) = 0$
and 
$\varphi_{\{13/2\}}(X_1^{(1)},X_2^{(2)},X_3^{(3)}) =
\varphi_{\{1/2/3\}}(X_1,X_2,X_3) =  \varphi(X_1) \varphi(X_2) \varphi(X_3)$
show that there is no universal constant $c$ satisfying
the requirement.
<!-- end exa-5 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
We already verified in Section~\ref{sssec:vmonotone} that 
  Dacko's V-monotone independence  \cite{Dacko:2019} satisfies the axioms of a
  spreadability system, but  is non-associative.
  On the other hand, it also
  falls into the framework of the tree operad of Jekel and Liu
  \cite{JekelLiu:2020:operad} with the corresponding cumulants
  and it is an interesting question how these cumulants are related.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- defi-12: body_md -->
Let $\pi=(P_1,P_2,\dots, P_p) \in \mathcal{OP}_n, \underline{t}=(t_1,\dots, t_p) \in \mathbb{R}^p, j \in[p]$.  We define the \emph{partial cumulant} to be the polynomial
$$
K_{\pi, P_j}^{(t_1,\dots, t_{j-1},1,t_{j+1}, \dots, t_p)}(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\left.\frac{\partial }{\partial t_j}\right\rvert_{t_j=0}\varphi_{\pi}^{\underline{t}}(X_1,\dots, X_n).
$$
<!-- end defi-12 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
Let $\pi=(P_1,P_2,\dots, P_p) \in \mathcal{OP}_n$, $\underline{t}=(t_1,\dots, t_p) \in \mathbb{R}^p$, $j \in [p]$. 
  Then 
  \begin{multline*}
    K_{\pi, P_j}^{(t_1,\dots, t_{j-1},1,t_{j+1}, \dots, t_p)}(X_1,\dots,X_n)
    \\
    = \sum_{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_{P_j}}\varphi_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},\sigma,P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}^{(t_1,\dots, t_{j-1},1, t_{j+1}, \dots, t_p)}(X_1,\dots, X_n)\, \widetilde{\mu}(\sigma, \hat{1}_{P_j}).  
  \end{multline*}
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm diff-eq} For $\pi =(P_1,P_2,\dots, P_p) \in \mathcal{OP}_n$,
  $\underline{t} =(t_1,t_2,\dots, t_p)$ and $j \in [p]$ we have 
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t_j} \varphi^{\underline{t}}_\pi(X_1,\dots, X_n) 
&= \sum_{\emptyset \neq A \subseteq P_j}K_{(P_1,\dots, P_{j-1}, A, P_j\setminus A, P_{j+1}, \dots, P_p),A}^{(t_1,\dots, t_{j-1}, 1, t_j, t_{j+1}, \dots, t_p)}(X_1,\dots, X_n)  \label{eq diff1}\\
&= \sum_{\emptyset \neq A \subseteq P_j}K_{(P_1,\dots, P_{j-1}, P_j\setminus A, A, P_{j+1}, \dots, P_p),A}^{(t_1,\dots, t_{j-1}, t_j,1, t_{j+1}, \dots, t_p)}(X_1,\dots, X_n). \label{eq diff2}
\end{align}
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The main ingredient here is the invariance principle of Lemma~\ref{lem:quasimeetshift}. 
  Recall the delta/dot operation from Definition~\ref{def:dot}\ref{eq:deltaAX}, 
  tensor notations from Section~\ref{Notation} and recall that for
  any partition $\pi=(P_1,P_2,\dots, P_p) \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ the multilinear map $ \varphi_\pi^{\underline{t}}\colon \mathcal{A}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ is identified with the linear lifting
  $\tilde{\varphi}_\pi^{\underline{t}}\colon \mathcal{A}^{\otimes n} \to \mathbb{C}$.
  Similar to \eqref{notation:linear},
  for a linear map $L\colon \mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}$ we
  we adopt the notation
  $L^{\otimes  P}\colon \mathcal{A}^{\otimes n} \to \mathcal{B}^{\otimes n}$ for the linear map
  \begin{equation*}
L^{\otimes P}=I\otimes I\otimes\dots\otimes L\otimes I\otimes \dots\otimes L\otimes I\otimes\dots\otimes L\otimes\dots\otimes I
  \end{equation*}
  with $L$ appearing exactly at position $j$ for every $j\in P$. 
  Let
  ${\mathbf X}=X_1\otimes X_2\otimes \dots\otimes X_n$, let $k + [m]:=\{k+1,k+2,\dots, k+m\}$ and let $e_j \in \mathbb{R}^p$ be the $j$th unit vector. Then, for each $j \in [p]$, 
  \begin{equation}\label{eq901}
   \varphi_\pi^{\underline{N}+me_j}(X_1,\dots, X_n) 
   =   \varphi_\pi^{\underline{N}+me_j}({\mathbf X})  
      = \varphi_\pi\left(      \left(\delta_{[N_j+m]}^{\otimes P_j} \prod_{i\ne j}
          \delta_{[N_i]}^{\otimes P_i}\right) ({\mathbf X})\right)
      ;
    \end{equation}
    after expansion we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq9010}
\delta_{[N_j+m]}^{\otimes P_j} = (\delta_{[N_j]}+\delta_{N_j+[m]})^{\otimes P_j}
= \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} \delta_{[N_j]}^{\otimes P_j \setminus A} \delta_{N_j+[m] }^{\otimes A}
\end{equation}
and thus \eqref{eq901} is equal to
\begin{align}\label{eq902}
&= \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_\pi\!\left(
        \left(\delta_{[N_j]}^{\otimes P_j \setminus A} \delta_{N_j+[m] }^{\otimes A}  \prod_{i\ne j} \delta_{[N_i]}^{\otimes P_i}\right) ({\mathbf X})
         \right).
\intertext{This is a sum of $\varphi_\pi$'s with entries $X_{k}^{(i_k)}, k\in[n]$, 
where the indices $i_k$ with $k\in A$ are strictly larger than the indices
  $i_k$ with $k\in P_j \setminus A$, and therefore we may split the block $P_j \in \pi$ into two parts:
}
\nonumber
&= \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},P_j\setminus A, A, P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}\left(
        \left( \delta_{[N_j]}^{\otimes P_j \setminus A} \delta_{N_j+[m] }^{\otimes A} \prod_{i\ne j} \delta_{[N_i]}^{\otimes P_i}\right) ({\mathbf X}) 
         \right). 
\intertext{
  Now by Lemma~\ref{lem:quasimeetshift} 
  the local shift in $A$ can be omitted without changing the value 
  and we obtain
}
\label{eq9030}
&=  \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},P_j\setminus A, A, P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}\left(
        \left( \delta_{[N_j]}^{\otimes P_j \setminus A} \delta_{[m]}^{\otimes A} \prod_{i\ne j} \delta_{[N_i]}^{\otimes P_i}\right) ({\mathbf X}) 
         \right)
\\
    &= \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},P_j\setminus A, A, P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}^{(N_1,N_2,\dots,N_{j-1},N_j,m,N_{j+1},\dots,N_p)}
      ({\mathbf X}).
      \nonumber
\end{align}
The analytic extension of this identity is
  \begin{align*}
    \varphi_\pi^{\underline{t}+se_j}({\mathbf X})
    &= \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},P_j\setminus A, A, P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}^{(t_1,t_2,\dots,t_{j-1},t_j,s,t_{j+1},\dots,t_p)}
       ({\mathbf X})\\
    &= \varphi_\pi^{\underline{t}}({\mathbf X})
       +
       \sum_{\emptyset\ne A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},P_j\setminus A,A, P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}^{(t_1,t_2,\dots,t_{j-1},t_j,s,t_{j+1},\dots,t_p)}
       ({\mathbf X}),  
  \end{align*}
  and the derivative satisfies the derived identity
 \eqref{eq diff2}: 
  $$
  \frac{\partial}{\partial t_j} \varphi_\pi^{\underline{t}}({\mathbf X})
  =
  \left.
    \frac{\partial}{\partial s}
  \right\rvert_{s=0}
  \varphi_\pi^{\underline{t}+se_j}({\mathbf X})
  = \sum_{\emptyset\ne A\subseteq P_j}
     K_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},P_j\setminus A,A,P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}^{(t_1,t_2,\dots,t_{j-1},t_j,1,t_{j+1},\dots,t_p)}
       ({\mathbf X}). 
  $$
  In order to prove the first differential equation \eqref{eq diff1}
  we replace \eqref{eq9010} by the complementary expansion
  \begin{equation*}
\delta_{[N_j+m]}^{\otimes P_j} = (\delta_{[m]}+\delta_{m+[N_j]})^{\otimes P_j}
= \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} \delta_{[m]}^{\otimes A} \delta_{m+[N_j]}^{\otimes P_j \setminus A}, 
\end{equation*}
and following the lines of \eqref{eq902}--\eqref{eq9030} we obtain 
\begin{multline*}
   \varphi_\pi^{\underline{N}+me_j}(X_1,\dots, X_n) \\
   \begin{aligned}[t]
&= \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_\pi\!\left(
        \left( \delta_{[m]}^{\otimes A} \delta_{m+[N_j]}^{\otimes P_j \setminus A}  \prod_{i\ne j} \delta_{[N_i]}^{\otimes P_i}\right) ({\mathbf X})
         \right) 
   \\
  &=  \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},A, P_j\setminus A, P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}\left(
        \left( \delta_{[m]}^{\otimes A} \delta_{[N_j]}^{\otimes P_j \setminus A}\prod_{i\ne j} \delta_{[N_i]}^{\otimes P_i}\right) ({\mathbf X}) 
         \right)
\\
    &= \sum_{A\subseteq P_j} 
       \varphi_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{j-1},A,P_j\setminus A, P_{j+1},\dots,P_p)}^{(N_1,N_2,\dots,N_{j-1},m,N_j,N_{j+1},\dots,N_p)}
       ({\mathbf X}).      
   \end{aligned}
\end{multline*}
By analytic continuation, we may replace $m$ and $N_i$ with $s$ and $t_i$ respectively. Taking the derivative with respect to $s$ at $0$ we obtain \eqref{eq diff1}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
In the case of exchangeability both differential equations coincide.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- exa-6: body_md -->
Consider the tensor spreadability system   $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{T}}$.
  It satisfies the factorization property   \eqref{eq:otimesindep:factor}
  and therefore 
  \begin{equation*}
    \varphi_{(A,A^c)}^{(t_1,t_2)}(X_1,\dots, X_n) = \varphi^{t_1}(X_A)\, \varphi^{t_2}(X_{A^c}), 
  \end{equation*}
  so we get 
  \begin{equation*}
    K_{(A,A^c), A}^{(1,t_2)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) 
    = \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}\right\rvert_{t_1=0} \varphi^{t_1}(X_A) \,\varphi^{t_2}(X_{A^c}) 
    = K_{|A|}^{\mathrm{T}}(X_A)\, \varphi^{t_2}(X_{A^c}). 
  \end{equation*}
  The  identities in Theorem~\ref{thm diff-eq} (for $\pi=\hat{1}_n$) read
  \begin{equation}\label{eqTdiff}
    \frac{d}{d t} \varphi^t (X_1,\dots, X_n) = \sum_{\emptyset \neq A \subseteq [n]} K_{|A|}^{\mathrm{T}}(X_A) \,\varphi^{t}(X_{A^c}). 
  \end{equation}


This differential equation can be translated to (exponential) 
generating functions as follows.
Given a vector $\underline{u}=(u_1,u_2,\dots, u_n)$  of \emph{commuting} indeterminates 
and a vector $\underline{X}=(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)$ of random variables
we define the exponential moment generating function
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{F}_{\underline{X}}^t(\underline{u})
&:= 1+\sum_{\substack{(p_1,\dots, p_n) \in (\mathbb{N} \cup \{0\})^n \\  (p_1,\dots, p_n)\neq0}} 
  \frac{u_1^{p_1}\cdots u_n^{p_n}}{p_1! \cdots p_n!}\,
  \varphi^t(\underbrace{X_1,\dots, X_1}_{\text{$p_1$ times}}, \dots, \underbrace{X_n,\dots X_n}_{\text{$p_n$ times}})\\
&= [\varphi (e^{u_1 X_1} \cdots e^{u_n X_n})]^t
\end{align*}
and the exponential cumulant generating function as the logarithm of the previous
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{L}_{\underline{X}}(\underline{u})
&:=  \sum_{\substack{(p_1,\dots, p_n) \in (\mathbb{N} \cup \{0\})^n \\ (p_1,\dots, p_n)\neq0}} 
\frac{u_1^{p_1}\cdots u_n^{p_n}}{p_1! \cdots p_n!}
\,
K_{p_1+\dots +p_n}^{\mathrm{T}}(\underbrace{X_1,\dots, X_1}_{\text{$p_1$ times}}, \dots, \underbrace{X_n,\dots X_n}_{\text{$p_n$ times}})\\
&= \log[\mathcal{F}_{\underline{X}}^1(\underline{u})]. 
\end{align*}
Then one can prove that  
\begin{equation*}
\frac{d}{dt} \mathcal{F}_{\underline{X}}^t(\underline{u}) = \mathcal{L}_{\underline{X}}(\underline{u}) \, \mathcal{F}_{\underline{X}}^t(\underline{u}), 
\end{equation*}
which is equivalent to \eqref{eqTdiff}. Note that the functions $\mathcal{L}_{\underline{X}}(\underline{u})$ and $\mathcal{F}_{\underline{X}}^t(\underline{u})$ commute.
<!-- end exa-6 -->
<!-- exa-7: body_md -->
\label{ex:Boole} 
  In the Boolean spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{B}}$ we have
  \begin{equation*}
    \varphi_{(A,A^c)}^{(t_1,t_2)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)
    = \prod_{P \in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A)}\varphi^{t_1}(X_P) \prod_{Q\in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)}\varphi^{t_2}(X_Q).
  \end{equation*}
  where $\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A)$ is  the interval partition
  constructed in Definition~\ref{app:def:ncmax}
  and 
  consists of the contiguous subintervals of $A$.
  It follows that 
  \begin{equation*}
      K_{(A,A^c), A}^{(1,t_2)}(X_1,X_2\dots, X_n) 
      = 
      \begin{cases}
        K_{|A|}^{\mathrm{B}}(X_A)  \prod_{Q\in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)}\varphi^{t_2}(X_Q), & \text{if $|\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A)|=1$}, \\ 
        0, & \text{if $|\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A)|>1$}.  
      \end{cases}
  \end{equation*}
The identities in Theorem~\ref{thm diff-eq} (for $\pi=\hat{1}_n$) coincide
and read
\begin{equation}\label{eqBdiff}
\frac{d}{d t} \varphi^t (X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = \sum_{A: \text{~interval of~} [n]} K_{|A|}^{\mathrm{B}}(X_A) \prod_{Q\in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)}\varphi^{t}(X_Q). 
\end{equation}
This differential equation can be interpreted in terms of generating functions
in {\it noncommuting} indeterminates $z_1,\dots, z_n$. 
To this end we define noncommutative formal power series  
\begin{align*}
M_{\underline{X}}^t (\underline{z}) 
&=1 +
 \sum_{m=1}^\infty \sum_{i_1, \cdots, i_m = 1} ^n 
\varphi^t(X_{i_1},X_{i_2},\dots, X_{i_m})
\,z_{i_1}\cdots z_{i_m}
\intertext{and }
K_{\underline{X}}^{\mathrm{B}} (\underline{z}) 
&= \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\right\rvert_0 M_{(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)}^t (\underline{z}) \\
&= \sum_{m=1}^\infty \sum_{i_1, \cdots, i_m = 1} ^n 
K_m^{\mathrm{B}}(X_{i_1},\dots, X_{i_m})
\,
z_{i_1}\cdots z_{i_m}. 
\end{align*}
