Then differential equation \eqref{eqBdiff} is equivalent to the identity 
\begin{equation*}
\frac{d}{d t} M_{\underline{X}}^t(\underline{z}) 
= M_{\underline{X}}^t(\underline{z})\, K_{\underline{X}}^{\mathrm{B}} (\underline{z})\,  M_{\underline{X}}^t(\underline{z}). 
\end{equation*}
Note that $M_{\underline{X}}^t(\underline{z})$ and $K_{\underline{X}}^{\mathrm{B}} (\underline{z})$ do not commute.
<!-- end exa-7 -->
<!-- exa-8: body_md -->
\label{ex:monotone-diff-eq}
  Consider the monotone spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{M}}$.
  With the notation $\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A)$ introduced in 
  Definition~\ref{app:def:ncmax} we have
\begin{equation*}
\varphi_{(A,A^c)}^{(t_1,t_2)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = \varphi^{t_1}(X_A) \prod_{B \in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)} \varphi^{t_2}(X_B), 
\end{equation*}
using monotone independence.
Thus
\begin{align*}
  K_{(A,A^c), A}^{(1,t_2)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)
  &=  \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}\right\rvert_{t_1=0} \varphi^{t_1}(X_A)
    \prod_{B \in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)} \varphi^{t_2}(X_B)
    \\
    &= K_{|A|}^{\mathrm{M}}(X_A)\prod_{B \in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)} \varphi^{t_2}(X_B). 
\end{align*}
The first identity in Theorem~\ref{thm diff-eq} (for $\pi=\hat{1}_n$) reads 
\begin{equation}\label{eq diff m1}
\frac{d}{d t} \varphi^t (X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = \sum_{ \emptyset \neq A \subseteq [n]} K_{|A|}^{\mathrm{M}}(X_A) \prod_{B \in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)} \varphi^{t_2}(X_B), 
\end{equation}
which is exactly the first identity in \cite[Corollary 5.2]{HS11b}. 

On the other hand 
\begin{align*}
K_{(A^c,A), A}^{(t_1,1)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) 
&=  \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t_2}\right\rvert_{t_2=0} \varphi^{t_1}(X_A) \prod_{B \in \operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)} \varphi^{t_2}(X_B) \\
&= 
\begin{cases}
\varphi^{t_1}(X_A)\, K_{|A^c|}^{\mathrm{M}}(X_{A^c}), & \text{if $|\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)|=1$}, \\ 
0, & \text{if $|\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)|>1$}.   
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
 Condition $|\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A^c)|=1$ holds if and only if $A^c$ is an interval. Therefore, the second equality in Theorem~\ref{thm diff-eq} (for $\pi=\hat{1}_n$) reads 
\begin{equation}\label{eq diff m2}
\frac{d}{d t} \varphi^t (X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) 
= \sum_{B: \text{~interval of~} [n]} 
  K_{|B|}^{\mathrm{M}}(X_B)\,\varphi^t(X_{B^c}), 
\end{equation}
which is exactly the second equality in \cite[Corollary 5.2]{HS11b}. 

Results on generating functions in \cite{HS11b} 
correspond to these differential equations. For noncommutative indeterminates $z_1,\dots, z_n$, we define the cumulant generating function 
\begin{align*}
K_{\underline{X}}^{\mathrm{M}} (\underline{z}) 
&:= \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\right\rvert_0 M_{\underline{X}}^t (\underline{z}) \\
&= \sum_{m=1}^\infty \sum_{i_1,i_2, \cdots, i_m = 1} ^n 
    K_m^{\mathrm{M}}(X_{i_1}X_{i_2}\cdots X_{i_m})
    \,
    z_{i_1}z_{i_2}\cdots z_{i_m}. 
\end{align*}
Then it is shown in \cite[Theorem 6.3]{HS11b} that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq m convolution}
M_{\underline{X}}^{s+t} (\underline{z})  =  M_{\underline{X}}^t (\underline{z})\, M_{\underline{X}}^s (z_1M_{\underline{X}}^t (\underline{z}) , \dots, z_n M_{\underline{X}}^t (\underline{z}) ).  
\end{equation}
The partial derivatives of \eqref{eq m convolution} regarding $s$ at $0$ and $t$ at $0$ become \eqref{eq diff m1} and \eqref{eq diff m2}, respectively.
<!-- end exa-8 -->
<!-- exa-9: body_md -->
\label{ex:freediff}
Consider the free spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{F}}$. 
One can use the formula for products of free random variables
\cite[Theorem 14.4]{NicaSpeicher:2006:lectures} to show that 
for a nonempty subset $A\subseteq [n]$ we can expand
 \begin{equation*}
 \varphi_{(A,A^c)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = \varphi(X_A)\prod_{P\in \operatorname{\mathrm{\tilde{\iota}_{\max}}}(A^c)}\varphi(X_P) + R, 
 \end{equation*}
 where
 $\operatorname{\mathrm{\tilde{\iota}_{\max}}}(A^c)$ is the partition defined in
 Definition~\ref{app:def:ncmax} \ref{app:it:ncmax}
 and every term in $R$ has at least two factors from $A$, i.e., factors of the form $\varphi(X_{k_1}X_{k_2}\cdots X_{k_m})$, $k_1,k_2,\dots, k_m \in A$. For example,
$\varphi_{\{\{2,4\}, \{1,3,5\}\}}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_5) = \varphi(X_2 X_4)\, \varphi(X_1
X_5)\, \varphi(X_3) + R$,
where every term in $R$ contains the factor $\varphi(X_2)\,\varphi(X_4)$. 
 This implies that 
 \begin{equation*}
\varphi_{(A,A^c)}^{(t_1,t_2)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = \varphi^{t_1}(X_A)\prod_{P\in
  \operatorname{\mathrm{\tilde{\iota}_{\max}}}(A^c)}\varphi^{t_2}(X_P) +O(t_1^2) \qquad \text{as $t_1\to0$}, 
\end{equation*}
so by taking the partial derivative $ \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}\right\rvert_{t_1=0}$ we get 
\begin{equation*}
K_{(A,A^c), A}^{(1,t_2)}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = K_{|A|}^{\mathrm{F}}(X_A)\prod_{P\in \operatorname{\mathrm{\tilde{\iota}_{\max}}}(A^c)}\varphi^{t_2}(X_P).   
\end{equation*}
This yields the differential equation 
\begin{equation}\label{diff:free}
\frac{d}{d t} \varphi^t (X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = \sum_{\emptyset \neq A \subseteq [n]} K_{|A|}^{\mathrm{F}}(X_A)\prod_{P\in \operatorname{\mathrm{\tilde{\iota}_{\max}}}(A^c)}\varphi^t(X_P),   
\end{equation}
which is similar to the monotone case \eqref{eq diff m1}. 

Denote by $\underline{z}=(z_1,z_2, \dots, z_n)$ a vector of noncommuting indeterminates and
by $\underline{X}=(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)$ a random vector. 
In order to obtain a differential equation we need in
addition the two-sided generating function
\begin{equation*}
\tilde{M}^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z},w):= \sum_{p,q=0}^\infty\sum_{\substack{i_1,i_2,\dots, i_p \in[n] \\ j_1,j_2,\dots, j_q \in[n]}} \varphi^t(X_{i_1},X_{i_2}, \dots, X_{i_p}, X_{j_1},X_{j_2}, \dots, X_{j_q})\,z_{i_1}z_{i_2}\cdots z_{i_p}w z_{j_1}z_{j_2}\cdots z_{j_q} 
\end{equation*}
as well as the $R$-transform
\begin{equation*}
R_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z})=\sum_{j=1}^\infty \sum_{i_1, \cdots, i_j = 1} ^n K_j^{\mathrm{F}}(X_{i_1},X_{i_2},\cdots, X_{i_j})\,z_{i_1}z_{i_2}\cdots z_{i_j}. 
\end{equation*}
After some computations we infer from \eqref{diff:free} that 
\begin{equation}\label{diff:free2}
\frac{\partial }{\partial t} M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z})
  = \tilde{M}^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z}, R(z_1M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z}),z_2 M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z}) ,\dots, z_n M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z})) (M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z}))^{-1}). 
\end{equation}
Note that by \cite[Corollary 16.16]{NicaSpeicher:2006:lectures} the second argument can be written as
\begin{equation*}
R(z_1 M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z}), z_2 M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z}) ,\dots, z_n M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z}))\,(M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z}))^{-1} =\frac{1- M^t_{\underline{X}}(\underline{z})^{-1}}{t}.
\end{equation*}
When $n=1$ the differential equation \eqref{diff:free2} is equivalent to the generalized complex Burgers equation (see \cite[p.\ 343]{V86}) 
\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial }{\partial t} G^t_{X}(z) + \frac{R_X(G_X^t(z))}{G^t_X(z)} \frac{\partial }{\partial z} G^t_{X}(z)=0, 
\end{equation*}
where $G^t_X$ is the Cauchy transform
\begin{equation*} 
G^t_X(z)= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \varphi^t(\underbrace{X,\dots,X}_{\text{$n$ fold}}) \, z^{-n-1}. 
\end{equation*}
<!-- end exa-9 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:mixedvanish}
  Let $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$ be a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps and 
  $\mathcal{E}=(\mathcal{U},\tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ an exchangeability system for $\mathcal{A}$.
  Given a partition $\pi\in\mathcal{P}_n$ and a family
  $X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n\in \mathcal{A}$ such that there is a block
  $P\in \pi$ which can be partitioned into $P=P_1\dot\cup P_2$
  such that $\{X_i:i\in P_1\}$ and  $\{X_i:i\in P_2\}$ are
  independent in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:exchangeableindependence},
  we have $K_\pi(X_1,X_2\dots,X_n)=0$.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemma Weisner}
  In any lattice $(P,\leq)$ the M\"obius function satisfies the identity
  $$
  \sum_{\substack{x\\ x\wedge a=c}} \mu(x,b) =
  \begin{cases}
    \mu(c,b) & \text{if $a\geq b$}\\ 
    0 &\text{if $a\not\geq b$}.
  \end{cases}
  $$
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $\rho$ be the partition
obtained from $\pi$ by splitting the block $P$
as indicated in the proposition, then $\rho<\pi$ and by assumption
$\varphi_\sigma(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)=\varphi_{\sigma\wedge\rho}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)$
for any $\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n$; hence
\begin{align*}
K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)
&= \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n \\\sigma\leq\pi}} \varphi_\sigma(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)\, \mu_\mathcal{P}(\sigma,\pi) \\
&= \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_n \\\sigma\leq\pi}} \varphi_{\sigma\wedge\rho}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)\, \mu_\mathcal{P}(\sigma,\pi) \\
& =\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{P}_n} \varphi_\tau(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n) \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in\mathcal{P}_n\\ \sigma\wedge\rho =\tau}}\, \mu_\mathcal{P}(\sigma,\pi). 
\end{align*}
Now $\rho\not\geq \pi$ and the second case of Weisner's lemma applies.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- defi-13: body_md -->
\label{defi:weisnergoldberg}
  For $\tau,\eta \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ let
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:defi:weisner}
 w(\tau,\eta)&:=\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \curlywedge
    \eta=\tau}}
    \widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\hat{1}_n), 
             && \text{(Weisner coefficients)}
    \\
    \label{eq:defi:goldberg}    
g(\tau,\eta)&:=\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \geq
    \tau}}\widetilde{\zeta}(\tau,\sigma)\,w(\sigma,\eta), 
             &&\text{(Goldberg coefficients)}
  \end{align}
  and more generally for $\tau,\eta,\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$
  define the partitioned Weisner and Goldberg coefficients
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:defi:partitionedweisner}    
    w(\tau,\eta,\pi)
    &:=\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \curlywedge
    \eta=\tau\\ \sigma \leq \pi}} \widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\pi), 
    \\
    \label{eq:defi:partitionedgoldberg}        
    g(\tau,\eta,\pi)
                    &:=\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\  \sigma \geq \tau}}\widetilde{\zeta}(\tau,\sigma)\,w(\sigma,\eta,\pi).     
  \end{align}
<!-- end defi-13 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
\label{rem:weisnervanish}
  It follows from the properties of the quasi-meet operation
  (cf.~Proposition~\ref{app:prop:quasimeet}
  \ref{app:it:barpiwsi=barwbar} and 
  \ref{app:it:piwsi<pi})
  that both
  $w(\tau,\eta,\pi)$ and $g(\tau,\eta,\pi)$ vanish unless
  $\bar{\tau}\leq\bar{\eta}$ and $\tau\leq\pi$.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{cum-mom}
Let $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U},\tilde{\varphi}, (\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge 1})$ be a spreadability system for a given
  $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$.  Let $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$ and
  $(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n) \in \mathbb{N}^n$  be a tuple with kernel
  $\eta=\kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)\in\mathcal{OP}_n$.
  Then
  \begin{align}
    K_\pi(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)}, \ldots, X_n^{(i_n)})
    &= \sum_{\substack{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \tau\leq\pi\\ \bar{\tau}\leq\bar{\eta}}}
        \varphi_\tau(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) \, w(\tau,\eta,\pi)
      \label{eq:cum-mom}
    \\
    &= \sum_{\substack{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \tau\leq\pi\\ \bar{\tau}\leq\bar{\eta}}}
       K_\tau(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) \, g(\tau,\eta,\pi)
      \label{eq:cum-cum}      
      .
  \end{align}
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We proceed as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:mixedvanish}.
Expressing cumulants in terms of moments (see Theorem~\ref{thm:mc}), we have 
\begin{align*}
K_\pi(X_1^{(i_1)},X_2^{(i_2)}, \ldots, X_n^{(i_n)}) 
&= \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \leq \pi}}
\varphi_\sigma(X_1^{(i_1)}, X_2^{(i_2)},\ldots,X_n^{(i_n)})\,\widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\pi) \\
&=  \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \leq \pi}} \varphi_{\sigma\curlywedge\eta}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\, \widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\pi)  \\
&=\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_n}  \varphi_\tau(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,\biggl(\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma\curlywedge\eta =\tau, \sigma \leq \pi }} \widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\pi) \biggr) \\
&= \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_n} \varphi_\tau(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) \, w(\tau,\eta,\pi)
\\
\intertext{which is \eqref{eq:cum-mom}. Now substitute the moment-cumulant
  formula     \eqref{eq:phipi=sumKsi}   to obtain }
&=  \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_n} \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in\mathcal{OP}_n\\ \sigma \leq \tau}}K_\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) \, \widetilde{\zeta}(\sigma,\tau)\,w(\tau,\eta,\pi) \\
&=  \sum_{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n} K_\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) \,\biggl(\sum_{\substack{\tau \in\mathcal{OP}_n\\ \tau\geq\sigma}}\widetilde{\zeta}(\sigma,\tau)\,w(\tau,\eta,\pi)\biggr) \\
&=  \sum_{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n} K_\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)\,g(\sigma,\eta,\pi).  
\end{align*}
Finally Remark~\ref{rem:weisnervanish} applies and the sums \eqref{eq:cum-mom} and \eqref{eq:cum-cum}
can be restricted to $\tau\leq\pi$ and $\bar{\tau}\leq\bar{\eta}$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{cum vanishing} Let $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U},\tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i\ge1})$ be a spreadability system for a given
  $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$. A sequence of subalgebras $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{A}$, where 
  $I\subseteq \mathbb{N}$, is \emph{$\mathcal{S}$-independent} if and only if for any tuple $(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)\in I^n$, any random variables $(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)\in \mathcal{A}_{i_1} \times \mathcal{A}_{i_2} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{A}_{i_n}$ and any ordered set partition $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$, we have 
\begin{equation}\label{semi-vanishing1}
  K_\pi(X_1,X_2, \ldots, X_n)
  - \sum_{\substack{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_n\\ \tau\leq\pi}}
  K_\tau(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)
  \, g(\tau,\kappa(i_1,\dots,i_n),\pi) = 0.  
\end{equation}
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{semi-vanishing3}
We can also formulate the theorem in terms of moments; we only need to replace
\eqref{semi-vanishing1} by the equation
\begin{equation*}
  K_\pi(X_1,X_2, \ldots, X_n)
  - \sum_{\substack{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_n\\ \tau\leq\pi}}
\varphi_\tau(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) \, w(\tau,\kappa(i_1,\dots,i_n),\pi) = 0.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Fix a tuple $(i_1,\dots, i_n)$ with kernel
  $\eta=\kappa(i_1,\dots,i_n)$.
  Independence means that
  \begin{align*}
  \varphi_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)
    &= \varphi_{\pi\curlywedge\eta}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)
      \\
    &= \varphi_\pi(X_1^{(i_1)},X_2^{(i_2)},\dots,X_n^{(i_n)})
  \end{align*}
  for all $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$,
  and by M\"{o}bius inversion this is equivalent to the identity
  \begin{align*}
  K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)
    &= K_\pi(X_1^{(i_1)},X_2^{(i_2)},\dots,X_n^{(i_n)})
      \\
    &=
      \sum_{\substack{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_n\\ \tau\leq\pi}}
      K_\tau(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n) \, g(\tau,\kappa(i_1,\dots,i_n),\pi)
  \end{align*}
  for all $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
It is not obvious that Theorem~\ref{cum vanishing} generalizes Proposition~\ref{prop:mixedvanish}
(vanishing of mixed cumulants for $\mathcal{E}$-independent subalgebras).
In fact it implies a nontrivial identity: for any $ \tau,\eta,\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ such that $\eta\rfloor_P \neq \hat{1}_P$ for some $P\in\pi$, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq permute}
\sum_{h \in \mathfrak{S}_{|\tau|}} g(h(\tau), \eta, \pi)=0, 
\end{equation}
where $h(\tau)$ is the action of the permutation $h$ on the blocks of $\tau$. 
Similarly, Remark~\ref{semi-vanishing3} (or Proposition~\ref{cum-mom})
generalizes the vanishing of mixed cumulants for $\mathcal{E}$-independent
subalgebras. Consequently we must have  
\begin{equation}\label{eq permute2}
\sum_{h \in \mathfrak{S}_{|\tau|}} w(h(\tau), \eta, \pi)=0 
\end{equation}
under the same assumptions on $\tau,\eta,\pi.$
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- defi-14: body_md -->
A \emph{multiset} is a pair $(A,f)$ where $A$ is the \emph{underlying set} and $f:A\to\mathbb{N}$ is a
  function. The value $f(a)$ is called the \emph{multiplicity} of the element
  $a\in A$. Informally, a multiset is a set which contains multiple
  indistinguishable  copies of each of its elements. In the present paper
  multisets will always be based on integer  segments $A=[n]$ and
  in this case the tuple $(f(1),f(2),\dots,f(n))$ is called the 
  \emph{type} of the multiset.
  A \emph{permutation of a multiset} is a rearrangement of all its elements 
  where all multiplicities are preserved, i.e., a word with a prescribed total number
  of occurrences of each letter.
  The number of distinct permutations of a multiset of type
  $(f_1,f_2,\dots,f_n)$ is given by the multinomial coefficient
  $$
  \binom{f_1+f_2+\dotsm+ f_n}{f_1,f_2,\dots,f_n}. 
  $$
  A \emph{proper set} is a multiset of type $(1,1,\dots,1)$ and we recover
  the number of its permutations as $n!$.
<!-- end defi-14 -->
<!-- defi-15: body_md -->
\label{def:desc}
  Let $\sigma=w_1w_2\dots w_s$ be a permutation of a multiset
  of type $(f_1,f_2,\dots,f_n)$ where $s=f_1+f_2+\dotsm+ f_n$.
  An index $1\leq i\leq s-1$ is called a
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*)]
   \item 
    \emph{descent} (or \emph{drop} or
    \emph{fall}) if $w_i>w_{i+1}$. 
   \item 
    \emph{plateau} (or \emph{level}) if $w_i=w_{i+1}$.
   \item 
    \emph{ascent} (or \emph{rise}) if $w_i<w_{i+1}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We denote these sets by
  \begin{align*}
    \operatorname{Des}(\sigma)&=\operatorname{Des}((w_i)_{i=1}^s)=\{j\in [s-1]\mid w_j > w_{j+1} \},\\
    \operatorname{Pla}(\sigma)&=\operatorname{Pla}((w_i)_{i=1}^s)=\{j\in [s-1]\mid w_j = w_{j+1} \},\\
    \operatorname{Asc}(\sigma)&=\operatorname{Asc}((w_i)_{i=1}^s)=\{j\in [s-1]\mid w_j < w_{j+1} \} 
  \end{align*} 
  and
  the respective cardinalities, i.e., 
  the number of descents (ascents, plateaux respectively) of the multiset
  permutation $\sigma$,
  by
  \begin{align*}
  \operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(\sigma)=\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}((w_i)_{i=1}^s)&=\left\lvert \operatorname{Des}((w_i)_{i=1}^s) \right\rvert,\\
  \operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}(\sigma)=\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}((w_i)_{i=1}^s)&=\left\lvert \operatorname{Pla}((w_i)_{i=1}^s) \right\rvert, \\
  \operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\sigma)=\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}((w_i)_{i=1}^s)&=\left\lvert \operatorname{Asc}((w_i)_{i=1}^s) \right\rvert.
  \end{align*}
<!-- end defi-15 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
\
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=1cm]
\item Note that some authors also count $i=s$ as a descent and  $i=0$ as an ascent.
   \item Counting permutations by descents and ascents is a classic subject in
    combinatorics. In the case of descents of multiset permutations this is also
    known as \emph{Simon Newcomb's problem}
    \cite{Riordan:1958:combinatorial,DillonRoselle:1969:simon}.
  \end{enumerate}
 \item  Clearly every
  element except the last is either a descent, an ascent, or a plateau,
  and therefore
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:desplaasc+1}
    \left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert = \operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(\sigma)+\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}(\sigma)+\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\sigma) + 1  
    .
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- defi-16: body_md -->
\label{def:DFR} 
  To any pair of ordered set partitions $\tau,\eta\in\mathcal{OP}_n$ such that
  $\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta}$, 
  we associate a multiset on $[\left\lvert \eta \right\rvert]$ by setting 
  the multiplicity of $k\in \{1,2,\dots,\left\lvert \eta \right\rvert\}$ to be equal to the
  number of blocks of $\tau$ contained in the $k$-th block of $\eta$.
  Replacing every block of $\tau$ by the label of the block of $\eta$
  containing it we obtain a permutation of this multiset.
  We denote by $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)$, $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)$ and $\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}_\eta(\tau)$ 
  its statistics as defined in Definition~\ref{def:desc}.
More precisely,
  let $\tau,\eta\in\mathcal{OP}_n$ such that  $\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta}$. If $\eta=
  (E_1,E_2,\ldots,E_e)$, then the blocks of  $\bar{\tau}$ can be arranged
  $$
  \bar{\tau} = \{ E_{1,1},E_{1,2},\ldots, E_{1,l_1}, \ldots, E_{e,1},\ldots, E_{e,l_e}\}, 
  $$ 
  where each $E_i = \bigcup_{j=1}^{l_i} E_{i,j}$ is a disjoint union taken in
  canonical order of the subsets (i.e., sorted according to their minimal
  elements). So $\tau$ can be written as  
  $$
  \tau=(E_{m_1,n_1},E_{m_2,n_2}, \ldots, E_{m_s, n_s}), 
  $$
  which is a permutation of the blocks of $\bar{\tau}$. Then we denote by
  $\operatorname{Des}_\eta(\tau), \operatorname{Pla}_\eta(\tau)$ and $\operatorname{Asc}_\eta(\tau)$ respectively, 
  the sets
  \begin{align*}
    \operatorname{Des}_\eta(\tau) &=\operatorname{Des}((m_i)_{i=1}^s), \\
    \operatorname{Pla}_\eta(\tau) &=   \operatorname{Pla}((m_i)_{i=1}^s), \\
    \operatorname{Asc}_\eta(\tau)  &= \operatorname{Asc}((m_i)_{i=1}^s)
  \end{align*}
  and by $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)$,
  $\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}_\eta(\tau)$ and $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)$ the respective cardinalities.
<!-- end defi-16 -->
<!-- exa-10: body_md -->
Consider the partitions $\eta=(E_1,E_2,E_3,E_4,E_5)\in \mathcal{OP}_{10}$ with blocks
  $E_1=\{5,8\}$, $E_2=\{9,10\}$, $E_3=\{3,6\}$, $E_4=\{1,2,4\}$, $E_5=\{7\}$,
  and 
  $\tau=(T_1, T_2, T_3,T_4,T_5,T_6,T_7,T_8)\in\mathcal{OP}_{10}$
  with blocks
  $T_1=\{3\}$, $T_2=\{6\}$, $T_3=\{1,4\}$, $T_4=\{7\}$, $T_5=\{10\}$, $T_6=\{5,8\}$,
  $T_7=\{9\}$, $T_8=\{2\}$. Then $\bar{\tau}\leq \bar{\eta}$. Now $T_1\subseteq
  E_3$ and thus $w_1=3$,  $T_2 \subseteq E_3$ and thus $w_2=3$, etc.; the
  multiset permutation thus induced on $\tau$ by $\eta$ is
  $$
  (w_i)_{i=1}^{8}=(3,3,4,5,2,1,2,4), 
  $$
  and the statistics are $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}((w_i)_{i=1}^8)=2$, $\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}((w_i)_{i=1}^8)=1$ and  $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}((w_i)_{i=1}^8)=4$.
<!-- end exa-10 -->
<!-- defi-17: body_md -->
Let $\sigma=(w_i)_{i=1}^s$ be a multiset permutation. An \emph{ascending
    (\emph{resp.}~descending) run}
  is a maximal contiguous subsequence $(w_i)_{i=l}^k$ which is strictly
  increasing (resp. decreasing). 
  Similarly, \emph{a level run} is a maximal subsequence $(w_i)_{i=j}^k$ such that
  $w_j=w_{j+1}=\cdots=w_k$.
<!-- end defi-17 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
Let $\sigma=(w_i)_{i=1}^s$ be a multiset permutation.   
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
   \item $\sigma$ can be decomposed uniquely into ascending runs
    separated by descents and plateaux. The number
    of ascending runs is equal to $s-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\sigma)$. 
   \item $\sigma$ can be decomposed uniquely into descending runs
    separated by ascents and plateaux. The number
    of descending runs is equal to $s-\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(\sigma)$. 
   \item $\sigma$ can be decomposed uniquely into level runs
    separated by ascents and descents. The number
    of level runs is equal to $s-\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}(\sigma)$. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We only prove (i).
  The claim is clearly true when $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}\sigma = s-1$, i.e., when the sequence is
  monotone increasing. Otherwise replacing any ascent by a descent or plateau
  splits an ascending run into two, i.e., increases the number of ascending
  runs by one.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-23: body_md -->
Suppose $\bar{\tau}=\bar{\eta}$, then
the blocks of  $\tau$ are a permutation of the blocks of $\eta$.
More precisely, if $\eta=(E_1,E_2,\dots,E_e)$ then
there is a permutation $h\in \mathfrak{S}_e$ 
such that $\tau=h(\eta)=(E_{h(1)},E_{h(2)}, \dots,E_{h(e)})$.
Then $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)$ and 
$\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)$ coincide with $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(h)$ and $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(h)$,
where the latter quantities are the numbers of descents and ascents of the
permutation $h$, respectively. See 
\cite{Bona:2012:combinatorics,Brenti:1993:permutation,Reutenauer:1993:freeLiealg}
and \cite[p.~25]{Stanley:1986:enumerative1}
for the uses of  $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(h)$ and
$\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(h)$ in the context of symmetric groups.
<!-- end remark-23 -->
<!-- exa-11: body_md -->
The  statistics of the sequence $(m_i)_{i=1}^9=(1,1,3,5,5,5,4,1,4)$
  are as follows:
  $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}((m_i)_{i=1}^9)=2$, $\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}((m_i)_{i=1}^9)=3$ and 
$\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}((m_i)_{i=1}^9)=3$. 
The decomposition into ascending runs is given by 
$$
(1), (1,3,5), (5), (5), (4), (1,4), 
$$
the decomposition into level runs is 
$$
(1,1), (3), (5,5,5), (4), (1), (4)
$$
and the decomposition into descending runs is 
$$
(1),(1),(3),(5),(5),(5,4,1),(4).
$$
<!-- end exa-11 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem7}
Let $\eta, \tau \in\mathcal{OP}_n$ such that $\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta}$, 
then there is an ordered set partition $\sigma_{\mathrm{max}}^{\mathrm{asc}}(\tau,\eta)$ such that 
$$
\{\sigma \in\mathcal{OP}_n \mid \sigma \curlywedge \eta =\tau \} =[\tau, \sigma_{\mathrm{max}}^{\mathrm{asc}}(\tau,\eta)]. 
$$
and the
restriction of the mapping $\Psi$ in Proposition~\ref{app:prop:OSPintervals}
establishes a poset isomorphism
$$
\{\sigma \in\mathcal{OP}_n \mid \sigma \curlywedge \eta =\tau \}  \to \mathcal{I}_{p_1} \times \mathcal{I}_{p_2} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{I}_{p_t}, 
$$
where $1 \leq p_i \leq n$ are the lengths of the ascending runs of the sequence $(m_i)_{i=1}^s$ from Definition~\ref{def:DFR} and $t=\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)$.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $\eta=(E_1,E_2,\ldots,E_e)$ and write
  $\tau=(E_{m_1,n_1},E_{m_2,n_2}, \ldots, E_{m_s, n_s})$
  as in Definition~\ref{def:DFR}.
  From Proposition~\ref{app:prop:quasimeet} we infer that  
  any partition $\sigma\in\mathcal{OP}_n$  such that $\sigma\curlywedge\eta=\tau$ 
  satisfies $\sigma \geq \tau$.
   From Proposition~\ref{app:prop:OSPintervals} we infer that there is an interval partition 
$\lambda=(L_1,L_2,\ldots, L_l) \in \mathcal{I}_{s}$ such that 
$$
\sigma=\biggl(\bigcup_{i\in L_1} E_{m_i,n_i},\bigcup_{i\in L_2} E_{m_i,n_i}, \ldots, \bigcup_{i\in L_l} E_{m_i,n_i}\biggr). 
$$ 
In order that $ \sigma \curlywedge \eta =\tau$ it is necessary and sufficient
that every block $L\in\lambda$, say $L=\{a+1, a+2, \ldots,a+b\}$, 
induces a strictly increasing sequence $m_{a+1} < m_{a+2}< \cdots <m_{a+b}$.


Let $(m_i)_{i=1}^{i_1}, (m_i)_{i=i_1+1}^{i_2},\ldots,
(m_i)_{i=i_{t-1}+1}^s$ be the decomposition of $(m_i)_{i=1}^s$ into ascending
runs. This decomposition defines the interval blocks $A_j:= \{i_{j-1}+1, i_{j-1}+2,\ldots,
i_j\}$ ($i_0=0,i_t=s$) and hence defines an interval partition $\alpha =
(A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_t)$. The interval partition $\lambda$ consists of
increasing intervals and therefore is finer than $\alpha$.
Thus we have an isomorphism
$$
\{\sigma \in\mathcal{OP}_n \mid \sigma \curlywedge \eta =\tau \}  \to \mathcal{I}_{A_1} \times\mathcal{I}_{A_2} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{I}_{A_t}
$$
via the restriction of the map $\Psi\rfloor_{[\tau,\hat{1}_n]}$ from Proposition~\ref{app:prop:OSPintervals}. The number $t=\left\lvert \alpha \right\rvert$ is equal to $\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)$, the integers $p_j$ are the cardinalities of $A_j$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{max}}^{\mathrm{asc}}(\tau,\eta)$ is the ordered set partition corresponding to $\lambda =\alpha$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:Weisner}     \  
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item\label{it:Weis1}
  For $\tau,\eta \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ the Weisner coefficient
  \eqref{eq:defi:weisner} is 
 \begin{equation}
   \label{eq:weisnercoeff}
w(\tau,\eta)
= 
\begin{cases}\displaystyle
\int_{-1}^0 x^{\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert -\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)-1}(1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}\,dx=\frac{(-1)^{\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)-1}}{\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert\binom{\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert-1}{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}}, &\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta},\\
0, & \bar{\tau} \not\leq \bar{\eta}. 
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
\item\label{it:Weis2}  For $\tau,\eta,\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ the partitioned Weisner
 coefficient     \eqref{eq:defi:partitionedweisner}  is
 \begin{equation*}
  w(\tau,\eta,\pi)
= 
\begin{cases}\displaystyle
\prod_{P\in\pi} w(\tau\rfloor_P,\eta\rfloor_P), &\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta},~\tau \leq \pi,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases}
 \end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
\ref{it:Weis1}\,\, If $\bar{\tau} \not\leq \bar{\eta}$, then there is no
$\sigma$ such that $\sigma \curlywedge \eta=\tau$ and the sum is empty. 
Let us therefore assume henceforth that $\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta}$. 
We take up the end of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem7} where we
established the poset isomorphism
\begin{align*}
\{\sigma \in\mathcal{OP}_n \mid \sigma \curlywedge \eta=\tau \} &
 \cong\mathcal{I}_{p_1} \times \mathcal{I}_{p_2} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{I}_{p_t} \\
& \cong \mathcal{B}_{p_1-1} \times \mathcal{B}_{p_2-1} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{B}_{p_t-1} \\
& \cong \mathcal{B}_{p_1+\cdots+p_t   -t}, 
\end{align*}
where the second isomorphism follows from Proposition~\ref{app:prop:interval-Boolean} and $p_i$ denotes the length of the $i$-th ascending run.
The latter contains $p_i-1$ rises and therefore the total number of
ascents is 
$\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau) = p_1+p_2+\cdots +p_t-t$.
In the identification above, a partition $\sigma$ is mapped to a subset 
$A\subseteq [p_1+p_2+\cdots+p_t-t]$ 
with  $\left\lvert A \right\rvert = \left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-t$ elements and we have
\begin{equation*}
\widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\hat{1}_n)= \frac{(-1)^{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-1}}{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert} = \frac{(-1)^{\left\lvert A \right\rvert+t-1}}{\left\lvert A \right\rvert+t}. 
\end{equation*}
Performing the sum we obtain
\begin{align*}
\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \curlywedge \eta=\tau}}\widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\hat{1}_n)
&=  \sum_{A \subseteq [\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)]}\frac{(-1)^{\left\lvert A \right\rvert+t-1}}{\left\lvert A \right\rvert+t}\\
&= \sum_{k=0}^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}\binom{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}{k} \frac{(-1)^{k+t-1}}{k+t} \\
&= \int_{-1}^0 \sum_{k=0}^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}\binom{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}{k} x^{k+t-1}\,dx \\
&= \int_{-1}^0 x^{t-1} (1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}\,dx \\
&= (-1)^{t-1}B(t, \operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)+1),  
\end{align*}
where $B$ is the beta function $B(a,b)= \frac{\Gamma(a )\Gamma(b )}{\Gamma(a+b)}$
which can be written in terms of binomial coefficients as desired. 


\vspace{2mm}\noindent
\ref{it:Weis2}\,\, In order for the set $\{\sigma\in\mathcal{OP}_n \mid \sigma \leq \pi,~ \sigma
\curlywedge \eta=\tau\}$ to be nonempty, 
it is necessary that $\tau \leq \pi$ and $\bar{\tau}\leq \bar{\eta}$. We adopt
the notations from Definition~\ref{def:DFR}
and infer from Proposition~\ref{app:prop:OSPintervals} that there exists an
interval partition $\rho=(R_1,R_2,\dots,R_p) \in \mathcal{I}_{s}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\pi = (P_1,P_2,\dots,P_p)= \biggl(\bigcup_{i\in R_1} E_{m_i,n_i},\bigcup_{i\in R_2} E_{m_i,n_i}, \dots, \bigcup_{i\in R_p} E_{m_i,n_i}\biggr). 
\end{equation*}
If follows from Lemma~\ref{lem7} that $\sigma$ belongs to $[\tau,
\sigma_{\max{}}^{\mathrm{asc}}(\tau,\eta)]$.
In addition, $\sigma$ must satisfy $\sigma \leq \pi$. Hence, the ascending runs considered in Lemma~\ref{lem7} are split by the blocks of $\pi$.
More precisely, for each $k\in[p]$ we decompose $(m_i)_{i\in R_k}$ into
ascending runs, which give rise to the interval partition
$\gamma_k=(G_{k,1},\dots, G_{k,u_k}) \in \mathcal{I}_{R_k}$ where $G_{k,j}$ 
consists of the indices $i$ of the $j$-th ascending run of $(m_i)_{i\in R_k}$. 
Then
\begin{equation*}
\sigma_{\max{}}^{\mathrm{asc}}(\tau\rfloor_{P_k},\eta\rfloor_{P_k})= \biggl(\bigcup_{i\in G_{k,1}} E_{m_i,n_i},\bigcup_{i\in G_{k,2}} E_{m_i,n_i},\dots, \bigcup_{i\in G_{k,u_k}} E_{m_i,n_i}\biggr)
\end{equation*} 
and for each $P\in\pi$, we pick an arbitrary $\sigma_P \in\mathcal{OP}_P$ from the interval
$[\tau\rfloor_P, \sigma_{\max{}}^{\mathrm{asc}}(\tau\rfloor_P,\eta\rfloor_P)]$,
concatenate them and obtain 
$\sigma=\sigma_{P_1} \sigma_{P_2}\cdots\sigma_{P_p} \in \mathcal{OP}_n$.
Since $\widetilde{\mu}(\sigma,\pi)$ is the product of
$\frac{(-1)^{\#(\sigma\rfloor_P)-1}}{\#(\sigma\rfloor_P)}$ over
$P\in\pi$, the conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem8}
Let $\eta, \tau \in\mathcal{OP}_n$ such that $\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta}$, then the
restriction of the map $\Psi\rfloor_{[\tau,\hat{1}_n]}$ from
Proposition~\ref{app:prop:OSPintervals} establishes a poset isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{iso flat}
\{\sigma \in\mathcal{OP}_n \mid \sigma \geq \tau, \bar{\sigma} \leq \bar{\eta} \}  \to
\mathcal{I}_{q_1} \times  \mathcal{I}_{q_2} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{I}_{q_r},  
\end{equation}
where $1 \leq q_i \leq n$ are the lengths of the level runs and
the number $r$ is equal to $\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}_\eta(\tau)$. 
In particular, there is an ordered set partition $\sigma_{\max{}}^{\mathrm{pla}}(\tau,\eta)$ such that 
$$
\{\sigma \in\mathcal{OP}_n \mid \sigma \geq \tau, \bar{\sigma} \leq \bar{\eta} \}  =[\tau, \sigma_{\max{}}^{\mathrm{pla}}(\tau,\eta)]. 
$$
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The proof is similar to that of Lemma~\ref{lem7}. 
Write $\tau=(E_{m_1,n_1},E_{m_2,n_2}, \ldots, E_{m_s, n_s})$ and
$\eta=(E_1,E_2,\ldots,E_e)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:DFR}. 
Let $\sigma \geq \tau$, then from Proposition~\ref{app:prop:OSPintervals} we infer
that there is an interval partition 
$\lambda=(L_1,L_2,\ldots, L_l) \in \mathcal{I}_{s}$ such that 
\begin{equation*}
\sigma=\biggl(\bigcup_{i\in L_1} E_{m_i,n_i},\bigcup_{i\in L_2} E_{m_i,n_i},  \ldots, \bigcup_{i\in L_l} E_{m_i,n_i}\biggr). 
\end{equation*}


Let $(m_i)_{i=1}^{i_1}, (m_i)_{i=i_1+1}^{i_2},\ldots, (m_i)_{i=i_{r-1}+1}^s$ be
the decomposition of $(m_i)_{i=1}^s$ into level runs. This decomposition
determines interval blocks $B_j:= (i_{j-1}+1,i_{j-1}+2,\ldots, i_j)$
($i_0=0,i_r=s$) and hence gives rise to an interval partition $\beta =
(B_1,B_2,\ldots,B_r)$. In order that $\bar{\sigma} \leq \bar{\eta}$, each $L_i$
connects only plateaux, which is equivalent to the condition that $\lambda\leq
\beta$.
Denoting by $q_j=\left\lvert B_j \right\rvert=i_j-i_{j-1}$, we get the isomorphism \eqref{iso flat}.  The ordered
set partition $\sigma_{\max}^{\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}}(\tau,\eta)$ corresponds to the 
choice $\lambda=\beta$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:goldberg}    \
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item\label{cum-cum1} For $\tau,\eta \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ the Goldberg coefficient
 \eqref{eq:defi:goldberg} evaluates to
\begin{equation*}
  g(\tau,\eta)
= 
\begin{cases}\displaystyle
\frac{1}{q_1! q_2! \cdots q_r!}\int_{-1}^0 x^{\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)}(1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}\prod_{j=1}^r P_{q_j}(x)\,dx, &\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta},\\
0, & \bar{\tau} \not\leq \bar{\eta}, 
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
where $r, q_1,q_2,\dots, q_r$ are the integers from Lemma~\ref{lem8},
$$
P_q(x)=\sum_{k=1}^q k! \, S(q,k)\, x^{k-1} = E_q(x,x+1),
$$
 $S(q,k)$ are the Stirling numbers of the second kind
and
$$
E_n(x,y)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_n}x^{\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}\sigma}y^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}\sigma}
$$
are the
\emph{homogeneous Eulerian polynomials}
\cite[p.~62]{Reutenauer:1993:freeLiealg}.
The first few polynomials are
\[
P_1(x)=1, \quad P_2(x)=2x +1,\quad P_3(x) = 6x^2 + 6x +1,\quad\dots
\]

\item\label{cum-cum2} 
 For $\tau,\eta,\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ the partitioned Goldberg coefficient
 coefficient     \eqref{eq:defi:partitionedgoldberg}  is
 \begin{equation*}
   g(\tau,\eta,\pi)
= 
   \begin{cases}\displaystyle
     \prod_{P\in\pi} g(\tau\rfloor_P,\eta\rfloor_P), &\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta},~\tau \leq \pi,\\
     0, & \text{otherwise}. 
   \end{cases}
 \end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
The name ``Goldberg coefficients'' originates from the
  Campbell-Baker-Hausdorff formula, see Section~\ref{sec:freeLiealg} below,
  in particular Theorem~\ref{thm:coefficient}.
  Some examples of $g(\tau,\eta)$ will be computed in Example~\ref{exa:GB}.
<!-- end remark-24 -->
<!-- remark-25: body_md -->
\label{rem:Frobenius}
  The expansion of $P_q(x)$ in terms of Stirling coefficients was first proved
  by Frobenius \cite[Theorem~E, p.~244]{Comtet:1974:advanced}.
<!-- end remark-25 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
\ref{cum-cum1}\,\, 
If $\bar{\tau} \not\leq \bar{\eta}$, then $w(\sigma,\eta)=0$ for all $\sigma \geq \tau$ and so $g(\tau,\eta)=0$. Assume hereafter that $\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta}$. 
From Lemma~\ref{lem8} we have the isomorphism 
\begin{align*}
\{\sigma \in\mathcal{OP}_n \mid \sigma \geq \tau, \bar{\sigma} \leq \bar{\eta} \}
&\cong \mathcal{I}_{q_1} \times \mathcal{I}_{q_2} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{I}_{q_r}, \\
\sigma &\mapsto (\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_r). 
\end{align*}
Since $r=\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}_\eta(\tau)=\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)+\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)+1$, we
have $\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)-1 = \sum_{i=1}^r
(\left\lvert \sigma_i \right\rvert-1)+\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)$. Note also that $[\tau:\sigma]!
=\prod_{i=1}^r \prod_{S\in\sigma_i}\left\lvert S \right\rvert!$.  Since $\sigma$ just connects the
blocks of a level run of $(m_i)_{i=1}^{\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert}$, it does not change the
number of ascents: $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\sigma)=\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)$ and we have 
\begin{multline*}
\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \geq \tau}}
  \widetilde{\zeta}(\tau,\sigma)
  \,
  w(\sigma,\eta)
  \\
  \begin{aligned}[t]
&=\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \geq \tau, \bar{\sigma} \leq \bar{\eta}}}\frac{1}{[\tau:\sigma]!} \int_{-1}^0 x^{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert -\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)-1}(1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}\,dx \\
&=  \sum_{(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_r) \in\mathcal{I}_{q_1} \times\mathcal{I}_{q_2} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{I}_{q_r}} \int_{-1}^0 x^{\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)}(1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}\prod_{i=1}^r\frac{x^{\left\lvert \sigma_i \right\rvert-1}}{\prod_{S\in\sigma_i }\left\lvert S \right\rvert!} dx \\ 
&=   \int_{-1}^0 x^{\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)}(1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}\prod_{i=1}^r\left(\sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{I}_{q_i}}\frac{x^{\left\lvert \rho \right\rvert-1}}{\prod_{R\in\rho}\left\lvert R \right\rvert!}\right) dx.  
  \end{aligned}
\end{multline*}
For $q\in\mathbb{N}$ we have  
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{I}_q}\frac{x^{\left\lvert \rho \right\rvert-1}}{\prod_{R\in\rho}\left\lvert R \right\rvert!} = \sum_{\substack{n_1+\cdots+n_k=q\\ n_i\geq1, k\geq1}}\frac{x^{k-1}}{n_1! \cdots n_k!}. 
\end{equation*}
For each fixed $k$, the sum $\sum_{\substack{n_1+\cdots+n_k=q\\
    n_i\geq1}}\frac{q!}{n_1! \cdots n_k!}$ is the number of ways of
distributing $q$ distinct objects among $k$ nonempty urns, so it equals  $k!
S(q,k)$ and the proof is complete.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent
\ref{cum-cum2}\,\, The idea of the proof is similar to Proposition~\ref{prop:Weisner}\ref{it:Weis2} and we omit the proof.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:vanish} Suppose $\tau,\eta\in\mathcal{OP}_n$ are such that $\bar{\tau}\leq \bar{\eta}$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item\label{vanish g} If $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)=\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)$ and $\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert$ is even then $g(\tau,\eta)=0$. 
\item\label{non vanish g} If $|\tau|$ is prime then $g(\tau,\eta) \neq0$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
\ref{vanish g} By \cite[Corollary 3.15]{Reutenauer:1993:freeLiealg}, the coefficient $g(\tau,\eta)$ of $K_\tau(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ vanishes if $q_1+\cdots +q_r +\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)+ \operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)-r$ is odd and $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)=\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)$. Since $\sum_{i=1}^r q_i = r +\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}_\eta(\tau)$ and $\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert= \operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)+\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)+\operatorname{\mathrm{pla}}_\eta(\tau)+1$, the conclusion follows. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent
\ref{non vanish g} The idea of the proof is taken from \cite{BV15}. Let $p:=\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert$. By definition and Proposition~\ref{prop:Weisner} we have 
\begin{align*}
g(\tau,\eta)
&=\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \geq \tau}}
   \widetilde{\zeta}(\tau,\sigma)\,w(\sigma,\eta) 
 =\sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma \geq \tau}}
    \frac{1}{[\tau:\sigma]!} \frac{(-1)^{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\sigma)-1}}{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert\binom{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-1}{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\sigma)}} \\
&=  \frac{(-1)^{p-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)-1}}{p\binom{p-1}{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)}} 
  + \sum_{\substack{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_n \\ \sigma > \tau}} 
    \frac{1}{[\tau:\sigma]!} 
    \frac{(-1)^{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\sigma)-1}}{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert\binom{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-1}{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\sigma)}}. 
\end{align*}
Since the number $[\tau:\sigma]!
\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert\binom{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-1}{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\sigma)}$ never contains $p$ as a
factor for any $\sigma >\tau$,  $g(\tau,\eta)$ is nonzero.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-26: body_md -->
It is a difficult problem to characterize vanishing Goldberg coefficients.  
  The criterion  \ref{vanish g} from Proposition~\ref{prop:vanish} above
  does not cover all cases,
  for example one can show that $g(\tau,\eta)=0$ for
  $\tau=(\{3\},\{4\},\{2\},\{1\}), \eta=(\{1,2,3\},\{4\})$,
  although the pair $(\tau,\eta)$ does not satisfy the assumption of the criterion.
  More information about Goldberg coefficients can be found in
  \cite{Reutenauer:1993:freeLiealg,Thompson82}
  and in particular  \cite[Section IV]{BV15} concerning the question of vanishing coefficients.
<!-- end remark-26 -->
<!-- exa-12: body_md -->
\label{exa:GB} 
We will write the ordered kernel set partition $\kappa(i_1,\dots, i_n)$ simply
as $i_1i_2\dots i_n$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=1cm]
 \item 
  Take $\eta= 12$. We compute $g(12,12)$. Now $\tau=\eta$ so $m_1=1, m_2=2, r=2, q_1=q_2=1$. Hence $\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}_\eta(\tau)=0, \operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)=1$ and so
\begin{equation*}
g(12,12)= \frac{1}{1!1!}\int_{-1}^0 (1+x) \,dx=\frac{1}{2}. 
\end{equation*}
Similarly  we get $g(21,12)=-\frac{1}{2}, g(12,21)=-\frac{1}{2},
g(21,21)=\frac{1}{2}$ and hence
\begin{align*}
&K_{11}(X^{(1)},Y^{(2)}) = \frac{1}{2}K_{12}(X,Y)-\frac{1}{2} K_{21}(X,Y), \\
& K_{11}(X^{(2)}, Y^{(1)}) =  -\frac{1}{2}K_{12}(X,Y)+\frac{1}{2} K_{21}(X,Y). 
\end{align*}

In the most popular spreadability systems, like the tensor, free, Boolean or
monotone spreadability systems, partitioned cumulants factorize, e.g., 
$K_{12}(X,Y)=K_1(X)K_1(Y)$. 
Hence we get $K_{11}(X^{(1)},Y^{(2)}) =K_{11}(X^{(2)},Y^{(1)})=0$. 

\item 
We then consider the case $\eta=112= (\{1,2\},\{3\})$. The Goldberg coefficients can be nonzero only when $\bar{\tau} \leq \bar{\eta}$, so $\tau$ is one of 
$$
112, 221, 123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321.
$$ 
If $\tau=112$ then $g(112,112)=\frac{1}{2}$ by the same calculation as $g(12,12)$. If $\tau=221$ then again $g(221,112)= -\frac{1}{2}$. 
If $\tau=123$ then $m_1=1,m_2=1,m_3=2, r=2, q_1=2, q_2=1$. So 
\begin{equation*}
g(123,112) = \frac{1}{1!2!}\int_{-1}^0 (1+x) P_2(x) \, dx = \frac{1}{12}. 
\end{equation*}
If we take $\tau= 132$ then $m_1=1,m_2=2, m_3=1$, so $r=3,q_1=q_2=q_3=1$, $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}} = 1, \operatorname{\mathrm{des}}=1$. Thus we get 
\begin{equation*}
g(132,112) = \frac{1}{1!1!1!}\int_{-1}^0 x (1+x) \, dx = -\frac{1}{6}. 
\end{equation*}
If we take $\tau= 231$ then $m_1=2,m_2=1,m_3=1$. So $r=2, q_1=1, q_2=2$, $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}=0,\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}=1$. Hence 
\begin{equation*}
g(231,112) = \frac{1}{1!2!}\int_{-1}^0 x P_2(x) \, dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^0 x (2x+1)\, dx=\frac{1}{12}. 
\end{equation*}
Similarly we can compute the remaining Goldberg coefficients and get 
\begin{multline*}
  K_{111}(X^{(1)},Y^{(1)},Z^{(2)})
   = \frac{1}{2} K_{112} -\frac{1}{2} K_{221} + \frac{1}{12} K_{123} -\frac{1}{6} K_{132} \\
    +\frac{1}{12}K_{213}+\frac{1}{12} K_{231} -\frac{1}{6}K_{312} + \frac{1}{12}K_{321}, 
\end{multline*}
where $X,Y,Z$ are omitted for simplicity. We can see that \eqref{eq permute} holds (now $\pi=111$): 
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}=0, \qquad  \frac{1}{12} -  \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{12}  - \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{12} =0.  
\end{equation*}

Again if the cumulants factorize then $K_{112}=K_{221}=K_{11}(X,Y)K_1(Z)$ and
$K_{123}=\cdots= K_{321} = K_1(X)K_1(Y)K_1(Z)$, so the mixed cumulant
$K_{111}(X^{(1)},Y^{(1)},Z^{(2)})$ vanishes.  

Similarly one can compute $g(\tau, 121)$ for all $\tau$ such that $\bar{\tau} \leq \overline{121}$ and get 
\begin{multline*}
  K_{111}(X^{(1)},Y^{(2)},Z^{(1)})
  = \frac{1}{2} K_{121} -\frac{1}{2} K_{212} - \frac{1}{6} K_{123} +\frac{1}{12} K_{132} \\
+\frac{1}{12}K_{213}+\frac{1}{12} K_{231} +\frac{1}{12}K_{312} - \frac{1}{6}K_{321}. 
\end{multline*}

Now in the tensor, free or Boolean spreadability system the mixed cumulant
vanishes. However in the monotone spreadability system it does not:  $K_{212}$
vanishes identically since $212$ is not a monotone partition (see Proposition
\ref{prop19}) and therefore, in the monotone case we have 
\[
K_{111}(X^{(1)},Y^{(2)},Z^{(1)}) = \frac{1}{2}K_{121}(X,Y,Z)=\frac{1}{2} K_{11}(X,Z)K_1(Y)
\]
which does not vanish in general. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end exa-12 -->
<!-- exa-13: body_md -->
\label{exa:W} We can reuse some results from Example~\ref{exa:GB}. 

  \begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*., leftmargin=1cm]
   \item 
    If we take $\tau=\eta=12$ then $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)=1$ and so
    \begin{equation*}
      w(12,12)= \frac{(-1)^{2-1-1}}{2 \binom{1}{1}}=\frac{1}{2}. 
    \end{equation*}
    
   \item 
    Similarly if $\tau=21$ and  $\eta=12$ then $m_1=2, m_1=1$ so $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)=0$. 
    Therefore we get $w(21,12)=-\frac{1}{2}$. Similarly, $w(12,21)=-\frac{1}{2}, w(21,21)=\frac{1}{2}$. So 
    \begin{align*}
      K_{11}(X^{(1)},Y^{(2)}) &= \frac{1}{2}\varphi_{12}(X,Y)-\frac{1}{2} \varphi_{21}(X,Y), \\
      K_{11}(X^{(2)}, Y^{(1)}) &=  -\frac{1}{2}\varphi_{12}(X,Y)+\frac{1}{2} \varphi_{21}(X,Y). 
    \end{align*}
    In factorizing spreadability systems we have
    $\varphi_{12}(X,Y)=\varphi_{21}(X,Y)=\varphi_1(X)\,\varphi_1(Y)$ and hence $K_{11}(X^{(1)},Y^{(2)}) =K_{11}(X^{(2)},Y^{(1)})=0$. 

\item 
One can show that $w(112,112)=\frac{1}{2} = - w(221,112)$ by the same calculation as $w(12,12)$ and $w(21,12)$. 
If $\tau=123,\eta=112$ then $m_1=1,m_2=1,m_3=2$, so $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}} =1$ and  
\begin{equation*}
w(123,112) = \frac{(-1)^{3-1-1}}{3\binom{2}{1}} = -\frac{1}{6}. 
\end{equation*}
If we take $\tau= 231$ then $m_1=2,m_2=1,m_3=1$ and so $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}=0$. Hence 
\begin{equation*}
w(231,112) = \frac{(-1)^{3-0-1}}{3\binom{2}{0}}=\frac{1}{3}. 
\end{equation*}
Similarly we can compute the remaining Weisner coefficients and get 
\begin{multline*}
  K_{111}(X^{(1)},Y^{(1)},Z^{(2)})
  = \frac{1}{2} \varphi_{112} -\frac{1}{2} \varphi_{221} - \frac{1}{6} \varphi_{123} -\frac{1}{6} \varphi_{132} \\
-\frac{1}{6}\varphi_{213}+\frac{1}{3} \varphi_{231} -\frac{1}{6}\varphi_{312} + \frac{1}{3}\varphi_{321}, 
\end{multline*}
where $X,Y,Z$ are omitted for simplicity. We can see that \eqref{eq permute2} holds (now $\pi=111$): 
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}=0, \qquad  -\frac{1}{6} -  \frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{3}  - \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{3} =0.  
\end{equation*}
In factorizing spreadability systems the mixed cumulant $K_{111}(X^{(1)},Y^{(1)},Z^{(2)})$ vanishes by using the factorization of partitioned moments. 

\item 
Similarly one can compute $w(\tau, 121)$ for all $\tau$ such that $\bar{\tau} \leq \overline{121}$ and get 
\begin{multline*}
  K_{111}(X^{(1)},Y^{(2)},Z^{(1)})
  = \frac{1}{2} \varphi_{121} -\frac{1}{2} \varphi_{212} - \frac{1}{6} \varphi_{123} -\frac{1}{6} \varphi_{132} \\
+\frac{1}{3}\varphi_{213}-\frac{1}{6} \varphi_{231} +\frac{1}{3}\varphi_{312} - \frac{1}{6}\varphi_{321}. 
\end{multline*}
In the tensor, free or Boolean spreadability system mixed cumulants
vanishes, but in the monotone case in general they don't:
indeed $\varphi_{212}=\varphi(X)\varphi(Y)\varphi(Z)$ while
$\varphi_{121}=\varphi(X Z)\varphi(Y)$. Therefore, in the monotone case we have
\[
K_{111}(X^{(1)},Y^{(2)},Z^{(1)}) = \frac{1}{2}(\varphi_{121}-\varphi_{212})=\frac{1}{2}(\varphi(X Z)- \varphi(X)\varphi(Z)) \varphi(Y)
\]
which does not vanish in general. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end exa-13 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
The triple $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{\shuffle}}=\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(\mathcal{A})=(\mathcal{U}, 
\operatorname{\mathrm{conc}}_\infty,(\iota^{(j)})_{j=1}^\infty)$ defined above constitutes a spreadability system for $(\mathcal{A},\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}})$.
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Clearly $\tilde{\varphi}\circ \iota^{(i)}=\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}$ on
$\mathcal{A}$. The symmetry condition (\ref{eq:spreadability}) holds too since the value of
$\tilde{\varphi}$ only depends on the ordered kernel set partition of the upper indices.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
For $\pi = (P_1,P_2,\dots, P_p) \in \mathcal{OP}_n$, we have 
\[
K_\pi^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = K_{|P_1|}^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X_{P_1})\,  K_{|P_2|}^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X_{P_2}) \dotsm  K_{|P_p|}^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X_{P_p}). 
\]
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For $\pi=(P_1,P_2,\dots, P_p)\in\mathcal{OP}_n$, 
\begin{multline*}
  \varphi_\pi(N.X_1,N.X_2, \dots, N.X_n) \\
  \begin{aligned}
&= \sum_{i_1, i_2,\dots, i_n \in [N]} \varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n)}(X_1,X_2, \dots, X_n) \\
&= \sum_{i_1,i_2, \dots, i_n \in [N]}  X_{\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n) \rfloor_{P_1}} X_{\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n) \rfloor_{P_2}} \cdots X_{\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n) \rfloor_{P_p}}\\
&= \biggl(
 \sum_{\substack{i_k \in [N] \\ k\in P_1}}  X_{\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n)  \rfloor_{P_1}}
  \biggr)
  \biggl(
  \sum_{\substack{i_k \in [N] \\ k\in P_2}}  X_{\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n)  \rfloor_{P_2}}
  \biggr)
  \,\cdots\,
  \biggl(
  \sum_{\substack{i_k \in [N] \\ k\in P_p}} X_{\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n) \rfloor_{P_p}}
  \biggr)
\\
  &= \tilde{\varphi}\biggl(\prod_{i\in P_1}N.X_i\biggr)\,
     \tilde{\varphi}\biggl(\prod_{i\in P_2}N.X_i\biggr)\,
    \cdots\,
    \tilde{\varphi}\biggl(\prod_{i\in P_p}N.X_i\biggr). 
  \end{aligned}
\end{multline*}
We conclude by observing that the coefficient of $N^{p}$ is the product of the
linear coefficients of the factors.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:mc-NCT}
 For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ we have 
\[
K_n^{\mathrm{\shuffle}} (X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = \sum_{\pi =(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_k)\in \mathcal{OP}_n} \frac{(-1)^{|\pi|-1}}{|\pi|}X_{P_1} X_{P_2}\cdots X_{P_k}.  
\]
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- exa-14: body_md -->
The reader can easily verify that 
\begin{align*}
K_1^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X)&=X, \\
K_2^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X_1,X_2) &= \frac{1}{2}[X_1,X_2], \\
K_3^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X_1,X_2,X_3) &= \frac{1}{3} (X_1 X_2 X_3+X_3 X_2 X_1) \\
&\qquad- \frac{1}{6} (X_1 X_3 X_2 + X_2 X_1 X_3 + X_2 X_3 X_1 + X_3 X_1 X_2).   \notag
\end{align*}
<!-- end exa-14 -->
<!-- remark-27: body_md -->
We will see in Section~\ref{ssec:freemonoid} that $K_n^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}~(n\geq2)$ can be expressed
  as a sum of commutators, i.e., a Lie polynomial.
<!-- end remark-27 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{Thm:CBH-c}
  As formal power series on $\mathcal{A}$ we have the identity   
\begin{multline*}
\log(e^{a_1} e^{a_2}\cdots e^{a_n}) \\
= \sum
\frac{1}{p_1!p_2! \cdots p_n!}
    K^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}_{p_1+p_2+\cdots+p_n}(\underbrace{a_{1}, a_{1},\ldots, a_{1}}_{\text{$p_1$ times}},
    \underbrace{a_{2}, a_{2},\ldots, a_{2}}_{\text{$p_2$ times}},
    \ldots,
    \underbrace{a_{n},a_n,\ldots,a_{n}}_{\text{$p_n$  times}}).
  \end{multline*}
  where the sum runs over all $n$-tuples   $(p_1,p_2,\dots,p_n) \in
  (\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\})^n$ 
with the exception of the tuple $(0,0,\dots,0)$.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
First observe that the right hand side of the claimed identity
  is the coefficient of $N$ in the series
  \begin{multline}
    \label{eq:log1}
1+ \sum_{\substack{(p_1,p_2,\dots,p_n) \in (\mathbb{N}\cup
    \{0\})^n,\\(p_1,p_2,\dots,p_n) \neq (0,0,\dots,0)  }} \frac{1}{p_1!p_2!
  \cdots
  p_n!}\tilde{\varphi}((N.a_{1})^{p_1}(N.a_2)^{p_2}\cdots\,(N.a_{n})^{p_n})\\
\begin{aligned}
&= \tilde{\varphi}(e^{N.a_1}e^{N.a_2} \cdots \, e^{N.a_n})
\\
&=  \tilde{\varphi}
   (e^{a_1^{(1)}+a_1^{(2)}+\cdots + a_1^{(N)}}
   e^{a_2^{(1)}+a_2^{(2)}+\cdots + a_2^{(N)}}
   \cdots\, e^{a_n^{(1)}+a_n^{(2)}+\cdots + a_n^{(N)}}). 
\end{aligned}
 \end{multline}
Our construction implies that $a_i^{(j)}, j=1,2,3,\dots$ mutually commute for
different $j$ and so
$$
e^{a_i^{(1)}+a_i^{(2)}+\cdots + a_i^{(N)}} = e^{a_i^{(1)}} e^{a_i^{(2)}}\cdots
e^{a_i^{(N)}}
.
$$
Thus \eqref{eq:log1} can be factorized as follows:
\begin{multline*}
  \tilde{\varphi}(e^{a_1^{(1)}+a_1^{(2)}+\cdots + a_1^{(N)}}
  e^{a_2^{(1)}+a_2^{(2)}+\cdots + a_2^{(N)}}
  \cdots e^{a_n^{(1)}+a_n^{(2)}+\cdots + a_n^{(N)}})
  \\
=   \tilde{\varphi}((e^{a_1^{(1)}}e^{a_1^{(2)}}\cdots e^{a_1^{(N)}})( e^{a_2^{(1)}} e^{a_2^{(2)}}\cdots e^{a_2^{(N)}}) \cdots ( e^{a_n^{(1)}} e^{a_n^{(2)}}\cdots e^{a_n^{(N)}}) ). 
 \end{multline*}
 Now $\tilde{\varphi}$ simply rearranges the factors
 according to the upper index and
 the last expression equals 
 \begin{equation*}
(e^{a_1} e^{a_2}\cdots e^{a_n})^N. 
\end{equation*}
On the other hand,
\begin{align*}
  (e^{a_1} e^{a_2}\cdots e^{a_n})^N 
  &= e^{N\log(e^{a_1} e^{a_2}\cdots e^{a_n})} \\
  &= 1 + N \log(e^{a_1} e^{a_2}\cdots e^{a_n})
    + \frac{N^2}{2!}( \log(e^{a_1} e^{a_2}\cdots e^{a_n}))^2 + \dots
\end{align*}
and
we conclude by comparing the coefficient of $N$ in this series with the one in
\eqref{eq:log1}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-28: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{Thm:CBH-c} is similar to the well-known formula for the generating
function of multivariate cumulants from classical probability theory, 
\begin{multline*}
\log \operatorname{\mathbf{E}}[e^{z_1 X_1 +z_2 X_2 +\cdots +z_n X_n}] \\
=  \sum
\frac{z_1^{p_1}z_2^{p_2}\cdots z_n^{p_n}}{p_1!p_2! \cdots p_n!}
K^{\mathrm{T}}_{p_1+p_2+\cdots+p_n}(
  \underbrace{X_{1}, X_{1},\ldots,  X_{1}}_{\text{$p_1$  times}},
  \underbrace{X_{2}, X_{2},\ldots,  X_{2}}_{\text{$p_2$  times}},
\ldots, \underbrace{X_{n},X_n,\ldots,X_{n}}_{\text{$p_n$ times}}), 
\end{multline*}
where $X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n$ are $\mathbb{C}$-valued classical random variables and $z_1,z_2,\dots, z_n$ are commuting indeterminates.
<!-- end remark-28 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{NCT independence}   \ 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item\label{LieCum1} 
A sequence $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i=1}^\infty$ of subalgebras of $\mathcal{A}$ is
$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{\shuffle}}$-independent if and only if the subalgebras $\mathcal{A}_1,
\mathcal{A}_2, \dots$ commute mutually. This is obviously equivalent to
$K_2^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X,Y)=0$ whenever $X \in \mathcal{A}_i, Y\in \mathcal{A}_j$
with $i\neq j$.  

\item\label{LieCum2} 
For fixed $n \geq2$, if $\{X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n\} \subseteq \mathcal{A}$ splits into
two mutually commuting families then 
$$
K_n^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)=0
.
$$  
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- remark-29: body_md -->
\label{rem:commutativity=vanishing}    \   
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=1cm]
\item
    Additivity of Lie polynomials in commuting variables is well known,
    see \cite[p.~20]{Reutenauer:1993:freeLiealg}.
   \item 
    We have thus shown that
    \[
    \text{$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{\shuffle}}$-independence $\iff$ commutativity $\iff$ vanishing of mixed cumulants}.
    \]
    This example illustrates that in general vanishing of mixed cumulants does not imply exchangeability. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-29 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
\ref{LieCum1}\,\, Suppose that $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i=1}^\infty$ is $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{\shuffle}}$-independent. Let $\pi =\hat{1}_2, \rho = (\{2\},\{1\}) \in\mathcal{OP}_2$ and let $X \in \mathcal{A}_i, Y \in \mathcal{A}_j$ for fixed $i > j$. Then $\kappa(i,j)=\rho$ and 
\begin{equation*}
\varphi_\pi(X,Y) = X Y, \qquad \varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \rho}(X,Y) = Y X, 
\end{equation*}
and by $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{\shuffle}}$-independence these two must coincide, so $X Y = Y
X$. This shows that $[\mathcal{A}_i,\mathcal{A}_j]=0$.  Conversely, if the
subalgebras $\mathcal{A}_1, \mathcal{A}_2, \dots$ mutually commute then
for any $i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n \in \mathbb{N}$, any $X_k \in \mathcal{A}_{i_k},
k=1,2,\dots, n$ and any $\pi=(P_1,P_2,\dots, P_p) \in\mathcal{OP}_n$ we have
\begin{equation*}
\varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \rho}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) = (X_{P_1 \cap R_1} X_{P_1 \cap R_2} \cdots X_{P_1 \cap R_r} )  \cdots (X_{P_p \cap R_1} X_{P_p \cap R_2} \cdots X_{P_p \cap R_r})
\end{equation*}
where $\rho=\kappa(i_1,i_2,\dots, i_n)=(R_1,R_2,\dots, R_r)$.
Here $X_\emptyset$ is understood as the unit $\hat{1}_\mathcal{A}$. 
Now if $\{X_k \mid k \in R_i\}$ and $\{X_k \mid k \in R_j\}$ mutually commute
for distinct $i,j$ then for each $i =1,2,\dots, p$ we have
\begin{equation*}
X_{P_i \cap R_1} X_{P_i \cap R_2} \cdots X_{P_i \cap R_r} = X_{P_i},  
\end{equation*}
which shows that $\varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \rho}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n) =\varphi_{\pi}(X_1,X_2\dots, X_n) $. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent
\ref{LieCum2}\,\, Suppose that $\{X_i \mid i\in I\}$ and $\{X_i \mid i\in I^c\}$ commute with
each other and $\emptyset \subsetneq I \subsetneq \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Then, for
commuting indeterminates $z_1,\dots, z_n$, we have  
\begin{equation}\label{sum log}
 \log(e^{z_1 X_1} e^{z_2 X_2} \cdots e^{z_n X_n}) = \log\Bigl(\prod_{i \in I} e^{z_ i X_i}\Bigr) + \log\Bigl(\prod_{i \in I^c} e^{z_ iX_i}\Bigr), 
 \end{equation}
  where the products $\prod_{i \in I}, \prod_{i \in I^c}$ preserve the natural
  orders on $I,I^c$, respectively.   On the other hand, by Theorem~\ref{Thm:CBH-c}
  we have 
  \begin{multline}\label{CBH d}
    \log(e^{z_1 X_1}e^{z_2 X_2} \cdots e^{z_n X_n}) \\
    =
 \sum \frac{z_1^{p_1} z_2^{p_2} \cdots z_n^{p_n}}{p_1!p_2! \cdots p_n!}
 K^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}_{p_1+p_2+\cdots+p_n}(
 \underbrace{X_{1}, X_{1},\ldots, X_{1}}_{\text{$p_1$ times}},
 \underbrace{X_{2}, X_{2},\ldots, X_{2}}_{\text{$p_2$ times}},
 \ldots,
 \underbrace{X_{n},X_n,\ldots,X_{n}}_{\text{$p_n$ times}}).
\end{multline}
Comparing the coefficients of $z_1z_2\cdots z_n$ in \eqref{sum log} with those
of \eqref{CBH d}  we conclude that $K_n^{\mathrm{\shuffle}}(X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n)=0$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The specialization   $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{\shuffle}} (\mathbb{C}\langle{\mathbf{A}}\rangle)$
    of the  unshuffle spreadability system
    from Section~\ref{sec NCT}   for the ncps $(\mathbb{C}\langle{\mathbf{A}}\rangle,\text{Id})$
    is  called the \emph{free Lie spreadability system}  and denoted by $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FL}}({\mathbf{A}})$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- defi-18: body_md -->
Let $\Pi: \mathbb{C}\langle{\mathbf{A}}\rangle \to \mathbb{C}\langle{\mathbf{A}}\rangle$ be the map defined by 
$$
\Pi=\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} (\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)^{\ast k}, 
$$
where $\epsilon$ is regarded as an endomorphism of $\mathbb{C}\langle{\mathbf{A}}\rangle$.
<!-- end defi-18 -->
<!-- prop-17: body_md -->
\label{Hausdorff1}
Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n \in {\mathbf{A}}$. Then 
$$
\Pi(a_1a_2\cdots a_n) = \sum_{\pi = (P_1, P_2, \dots) \in \mathcal{OP}_n}
\frac{(-1)^{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert-1}}{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert} a_{P_1} a_{P_2}\cdots a_{P_{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}}. 
$$
<!-- end prop-17 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
From \eqref{eq:delta} we have 
\begin{align*}
\Pi(a_1a_2\cdots a_n) 
&= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} (\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)^{\ast k}(a_1a_2\cdots a_n)\\
  &=\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} (\operatorname{\mathrm{conc}}_k \circ (\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)^{\otimes k}\circ \delta_k)(a_1a_2\cdots a_n) \\
  &=\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k}
\sum_{(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_k)    \in \mathcal{OPP}_n}
\!\!(\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)(a_{P_1}) (\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)(a_{P_2}) \cdots (\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)(a_{P_k}). 
\end{align*}
Note that $(\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)(1)=0$ and $(\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)(w)=w$ for
$w\in{\mathbf{A}}^\ast\setminus\{1\}$. If $P_i=\emptyset$ for some $i$, then
the product $(\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)(a_{P_1}) (\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)(a_{P_2}) \cdots
(\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\epsilon)(a_{P_k})$ vanishes.
Therefore only proper ordered set partitions contribute to the sum, and in
particular the sum extends over $k \leq n$ only.  This proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:Hausdorff2}
Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n \in {\mathbf{A}}$ and let $K^{\mathrm{FL}}_\pi$ be the cumulants associated to the spreadability system $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FL}}$. Then 
$$
\Pi(a_1a_2\cdots a_n) = K^{\mathrm{FL}}_n(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n). 
$$
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- remark-30: body_md -->
\label{Rem:FL}   \
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=1cm] 
\item The space of \emph{Lie polynomials} $\mathcal{L}({\mathbf{A}})$ is the smallest subspace
 of $\mathbb{C}\langle{\mathbf{A}}\rangle$ that contains ${\mathbf{A}}$ and is closed with respect to the Lie bracket
 $[X,Y]=XY-YX$. It is well known that $\Pi$ is a Lie projector, i.e.,
 $\mathcal{L}({\mathbf{A}})=\Pi(\mathbb{C}\langle{\mathbf{A}}\rangle)$ \cite[Theorem 3.7]{Reutenauer:1993:freeLiealg}. 
So in the above setting cumulants with entries from ${\mathbf{A}}$ are exactly Lie
polynomials.

\item
 The values at words of higher order are given by convolution
powers of $\Pi$, i.e.,
\begin{equation*}
\Pi_k=\frac{1}{k!}\Pi^{\ast k},\qquad k\in\mathbb{N} 
\end{equation*}
(see \cite{Reutenauer:1993:freeLiealg}), 
and we can show that
\begin{equation*}
\Pi_k(a_1a_2\cdots a_n) =\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\substack{\pi\in \mathcal{OP}_n\\\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert=k}} K^{\mathrm{FL}}_\pi(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n),\qquad a_i\in{\mathbf{A}},~ i\in[n]. 
\end{equation*}
is the coefficient of $N^{k}$ appearing in $\tilde{\varphi}((N.a_1) (N.a_2)\cdots (N.a_n))$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:mc} and Proposition~\ref{ad}. In other words, 
\begin{equation*}
\tilde{\varphi}((N.a_1) (N.a_2)\cdots (N.a_n))= \sum_{k=1}^n N^k \Pi_k(a_1a_2\cdots a_n),\qquad a_i\in{\mathbf{A}},~ i\in[n]. 
\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-30 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem0123}
Let $\eta=(E_1,E_2,\dots,E_e)$ be an interval partition of $[n]$ where the blocks are in canonical order, i.e.\ if $s<t$ then $i<j$ for all $ i\in E_s, j\in E_t$. 
Then for any $X_i \in \mathbb{C}\langle{\mathbf{A}}\rangle$ and any $\pi\in \mathcal{OP}_n$, we have
$$
\varphi_{\pi \curlywedge \eta}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)=\varphi_{\pi}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n). 
$$
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The statement holds by definition because every block $P\in\pi$ is the concatenation
of $P\cap E_1, P\cap E_2, \dots, P\cap E_e$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- remark-31: body_md -->
Thus a sequence of distinct letters satisfies some partial independence, but it is not $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FL}}$-independent. Indeed, $(a_1,a_2)\in {\mathbf{A}} \times {\mathbf{A}}$ is $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FL}}$-independent if and only if $a_1=a_2$ by Proposition~\ref{NCT independence}.
<!-- end remark-31 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:coefficient}  
  Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ be distinct letters from the alphabet  ${\mathbf{A}}$, let $r\in\mathbb{N}$ and
  $q_j,i_j \in \mathbb{N}$ for $j\in [r]$ such that $i_j \neq i_{j+1}$ for $j\in[r-1]$. 
  Then the coefficient of the monomial $a_{i_1}^{q_1}a_{i_2}^{q_2}\cdots
a_{i_r}^{q_r}$ appearing in $\log(e^{a_1}\cdots e^{a_n})$ is given by 
\begin{equation*} \frac{1}{q_1!q_2!\cdots q_r!}\int_{-1}^0 x^{\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(\underline{i})} (1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\underline{i})} \prod_{j=1}^r P_{q_j}(x)\,dx, 
\end{equation*}
where $P_q(x)$ are the homogeneous Euler polynomials already encountered in Proposition~\ref{prop:goldberg}.
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
In order for a monomial $v=a_{i_1}^{q_1}a_{i_2}^{q_2}\cdots a_{i_r}^{q_r}$ to
  occur as a term in $\Pi(a_1^{p_1}a_2^{p_2}\cdots a_n^{p_n})$ it necessarily
  has to be a rearrangement of the word (= permutation of the multiset)
  $w=a_1^{p_1}a_2^{p_2}\dotsm a_n^{p_n}$, 
  since the projector in the CBH formula \eqref{CBH} does not
  change multiplicities and therefore
  every letter must occur the same number of times in $v$ and $w$. 
  
  Thus $p_k=\sum_{j\in B_k}q_j$ where  $B_k=\{j : i_j=k\}$.
  Let $p=p_1+p_2+\dots+p_n$ be the total length of $w$
  and $\eta=(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n)\in \mathcal{OI}_p$ be the ordered interval partition
  corresponding to the composition $(p_1,p_2,\dots,p_n)$, i.e.,
  $A_j=\{p_1+p_2+\dots+p_{j-1}+1,
  p_1+p_2+\dots+p_{j-1}+2,\dots,p_1+p_2+\dots+p_j\}$
  and $\left\lvert A_j \right\rvert=p_j$.

  From Theorem~\ref{thm:Hausdorff2} we infer
  \begin{align*}
    \Pi(a_{1}^{p_1}a_{2}^{p_2} \cdots a_{n}^{p_n})
    &=   K^{\mathrm{FL}}_{p}(\underbrace{a_1, a_1,\ldots, a_1}_{\text{$p_1$ times}},
                   \underbrace{a_2, a_2,\ldots, a_2}_{\text{$p_2$ times}},
                   \ldots,
      \underbrace{a_{n},a_{n},\ldots,a_{n}}_{\text{$p_n$ times}})
      \\
    & =:K_p^{\mathrm{FL}}(a_1^{\dots p_1},a_2^{\dots p_2}, \dots, a_n^{\dots p_n}). 
  \end{align*}

 Note that by Lemma~\ref{lem0123} we have
 $$
 \varphi_{\pi}(a_1^{\dots p_1},a_2^{\dots p_2}, \dots, a_n^{\dots p_n}) 
= \varphi_{\pi \curlywedge \eta}(a_1^{\dots p_1},a_2^{\dots p_2},
\dots,a_n^{\dots p_n})
$$
for any $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_p$
and 
thus
\begin{align*}
K^{\mathrm{FL}}_{p}(a_1^{\dots p_1},a_2^{\dots p_2}, \dots, a_n^{\dots p_n}) 
&= \sum_{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_p} \varphi_\sigma(a_1^{\dots p_1},a_2^{\dots p_2}, \dots, a_n^{\dots p_n}) 
\, \widetilde{\mu}(\sigma, \hat{1}_p)
  \\
&= \sum_{\sigma \in \mathcal{OP}_p} \varphi_{\sigma\curlywedge\eta}
   (a_1^{\dots p_1},a_2^{\dots p_2}, \dots, a_n^{\dots p_n}) 
   \, \widetilde{\mu}(\sigma, \hat{1}_p)\\
&= \sum_{\substack{\tau \in \mathcal{OP}_p \\ \bar{\tau}\leq \bar{\eta}}}
   \varphi_{\tau}(a_1^{\dots p_1},a_2^{\dots p_2}, \dots, a_n^{\dots p_n}) 
   \,w(\tau, \eta)
\end{align*}
by Proposition~\ref{prop:Weisner}.
Thus in order to determine the coefficient of $v$ we must
collect all ordered set partitions $\tau$ such that 
\begin{equation*} T_v =\{\tau\in\mathcal{OP}_p : \bar{\tau}\leq\bar{\eta}, 
 \varphi_{\tau}(a_1^{\dots p_1},a_2^{\dots p_2}, \dots, a_n^{\dots p_n}) = v 
\}
\end{equation*}  
and then sum up the corresponding values of $w(\tau,\eta)$.
Let us now investigate the structure of this set.
First note that $T_v$ is an order ideal: if $\tau\in T_v$ and $\tau'\leq \tau$,
then $\tau'\in T_v$, because every block of $\tau$ contains only repetitions
of one letter and further refinement of $\tau$ leaves the end result
$v$ invariant.
Moreover $T_v$ is the disjoint union of the principal ideals
$\operatorname{\downarrow\!}\tau_0=\{\tau : \tau\leq \tau_0\}$
where $\tau_0\in T_v$ is maximal.

The maximal partition $\tau_0$ arises as follows:
After application of $\varphi_\tau$ for $\tau\in T_v$
each factor $a_j^{p_j}$ is divided into pieces
$a_j^{q_l}$, $l\in B_j$ and the number of such subdivisions is
the multinomial coefficient
$$
\binom{p_j}{q_l : l\in B_j}
.
$$
These subdivisions are in one-to-one correspondence with
ordered set partitions of $A_j$ which, pieced together in the order of $j$,
give rise to a maximal ordered set partition $\tau_0\in T_v$.
Thus in total there are  as many maximal ordered set partitions
as there are subdivisions, namely 
\begin{equation*} \binom{p_1}{q_l:l\in B_1}
\binom{p_2}{q_l:l\in B_2}
\dotsm
\binom{p_n}{q_l:l\in B_n}
=
 \frac{p_1!p_2!\cdots p_n!}{q_1!q_2!\cdots q_r!}
.
\end{equation*}
By Proposition~\ref{app:prop:princideals} the principal 
ideal $\operatorname{\downarrow\!}\tau_0$ generated by a maximal ordered set partition $\tau_0$ 
is isomorphic to
$$
\mathcal{OP}_{q_1}\times\mathcal{OP}_{q_2}\times\dotsm\mathcal{OP}_{q_r}
$$
and in particular, all principal ideals are isomorphic.
Moreover the number of ascents is $\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau)=\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\underline{i})$
and does not depend on the choice of $\tau\in T_v$.
Thus all ideals $\operatorname{\downarrow\!}\tau_0$ deliver the same contribution
and as a consequence of the discussion above we are left with
$$
\sum_{\tau\in T_v} w(\tau,\eta)
=
 \frac{p_1!p_2!\cdots p_n!}{q_1!q_2!\cdots q_r!}
\sum_{\tau\leq\tau_0} w(\tau,\eta)
$$
for one fixed maximal element $\tau_0\in T_v$.

A canonical representative $\tau_0$ is obtained by concatenating
consecutive subintervals of length $q_j$ from $A_{i_j}$, $j=1,2,\dots,r$.
Let us now turn to the value of $w(\tau,\eta)$. 
As seen above, the numbers of both ascents and descents of $\tau$ 
only depend on those of the sequence $\underline{i}$
and since $\underline{i}$ has no plateaux we infer from \eqref{eq:desplaasc+1} 
that $r=\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(\underline{i}) + \operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\underline{i})+1$.
On the other hand, if we denote by $(\tau_1,\tau_2,\dots,\tau_r)$
the image of $\tau\in\operatorname{\downarrow\!}\tau_0$ 
under the isomorphism of Proposition~\ref{app:prop:princideals}
then the first exponent in formula    \eqref{eq:weisnercoeff}  of Proposition~\ref{prop:Weisner} becomes
$$
\left\lvert \tau \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}_\eta(\tau) - 1 
= \sum_{j=1}^r \left\lvert \tau_j \right\rvert-\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\underline{i}) - 1
= \sum_{j=1}^r (\left\lvert \tau_j \right\rvert-1) + \operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(\underline{i})
$$
and thus
$$
w(\tau,\eta) = \int_{-1}^0 x^{\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(\underline{i})}(1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\underline{i})} \prod_{j=1}^r x^{\left\lvert \tau_j \right\rvert-1} \, d x 
$$
and summing over the cartesian product yields the total value
$$
\sum_{\tau\in T_v} w(\tau,\eta)
=
 \frac{p_1!p_2!\cdots p_n!}{q_1!q_2!\cdots q_r!}
 \int_{-1}^0 x^{\operatorname{\mathrm{des}}(\underline{i})}(1+x)^{\operatorname{\mathrm{asc}}(\underline{i})} \prod_{j=1}^r
 \left(
   \sum_{\rho\in\mathcal{OP}_{q_j}}
   x^{\left\lvert \rho \right\rvert-1}
 \right)  d x
.
$$
Finally note that 
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal{OP}_{q}}x^{\left\lvert \rho \right\rvert-1}= \sum_{\sigma \in \mathcal{P}_{q}} \left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert!\, x^{\left\lvert \sigma \right\rvert-1} =\sum_{k=1}^{q} k!\, S(q,k)  x^{k-1}. 
\end{equation*}
is indeed the homogeneous Euler polynomial as claimed, 
see Remark~\ref{rem:Frobenius}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- remark-32: body_md -->
The authors were not able to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:coefficient}
  as a corollary of Propositions~\ref{cum-mom} and \eqref{prop:goldberg} although Goldberg coefficients appear in both formulas.
<!-- end remark-32 -->
<!-- defi-19: body_md -->
\ 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
\item An element $k \in[n]$ is called a singleton of $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n$ if $\{k\} \in \pi$. 
\item Let $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i \geq 1})$ be a
 spreadability system for a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A},
 \varphi)$. 
 We will say that the \emph{singleton condition holds for $\mathcal{S}$} if
 $\varphi_\pi(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)=0$ for every tuple $(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)$ and
 every partition $\pi$ containing a singleton $\{k\}$ such that
 $\varphi(X_k)=0$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-19 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
Assume that a spreadability system $(\mathcal{U}, \tilde{\varphi},(\iota^{(i)})_{i \geq 1})$ for a $\mathcal{B}$-ncps $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ satisfies the singleton condition. 
Assume $\varphi(X)=0$ and let $Y_N:=\frac{N.X}{\sqrt{N}}$. Then, for each $n \in\mathbb{N}$ and $\rho \in \mathcal{P}_n$, 
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\varphi_\rho(Y_N, Y_N, \dots, Y_N)=
\begin{cases}
\sum_{\substack{\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n^{(2)}\\ \pi\leq \rho}} \frac{1}{\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert!}\varphi_\pi(X,X,\ldots,X), &n \text{~is even},\\
0,&n\text{~is odd}. 
\end{cases}
\] 
where $\mathcal{OP}_n^{(2)}$ is the set of pair ordered set partitions, i.e.\ every block of $\pi \in \mathcal{OP}_n^{(2)}$ contains exactly 2 entries.
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Note that the following holds: if $\pi$ has a singleton at $k$ and $\varphi(X_k)=0$, then 
\begin{equation*}
K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)=0. 
\end{equation*}
This holds because $K_\pi(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)$ is the coefficient of $N$ in $\varphi_\pi(N.X_1,N.X_2,\ldots,N.X_n)$, and 
\begin{equation*}
\varphi_\pi(N.X_1,N.X_2,\ldots,N.X_n)=\sum_{i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n\in[n]}\varphi_{\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)}(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)=0
\end{equation*} because each 
$\pi\curlywedge \kappa(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)$ has a singleton at $k$. 

Now multilinearity and extensivity of cumulants imply
\begin{equation*}
K_\pi(Y_N,Y_N,\ldots,Y_N)= N^{-\frac{n}{2}+\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert}K_\pi(X,X,\ldots,X). 
\end{equation*}
If $\pi$ has a singleton, this is zero. If $\pi$ does not have a singleton nor $\pi$ is not a pair ordered set partition, then $\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert<\frac{n}{2}$. Therefore,  
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{N\to\infty}K_\pi(Y_N,Y_N,\ldots,Y_N)= 
\begin{cases}
K_\pi(X,X,\ldots,X),&\text{if~$n$ is even and~}\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n^{(2)}, \\
0, &\text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\end{equation*}
If $\pi\in\mathcal{OP}_n^{(2)}$, then $K_\pi(X,X,\ldots, X)= \varphi_\pi(X,X,\ldots,X)$
from Theorem~\ref{thm:mc} because the expectations $\varphi_\sigma(X,X,\ldots,X)$ all
vanish for $\sigma <\pi$ from the singleton condition. Finally, from Theorem
\ref{thm:mc}, we obtain the conclusion.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A \emph{set partition}, or simply partition, of a finite set $A$ is a set of mutually disjoint subsets
$\pi=\{P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_k\}$ such that $\cup_{i=1}^k P_i = A$.  
The number $k$ is the \emph{size} of the partition and denoted by $\left\lvert \pi \right\rvert$. 
The elements $P\in\pi$ are called \textit{blocks} of $\pi$.
The set of partitions of $A$ is denoted by $\mathcal{P}_A.$ 
We are mostly concerned with the case $A=[n]$
and in this case $\mathcal{P}_{[n]}$ is abbreviated to $\mathcal{P}_n$
and called (set) \textit{partitions of order $n$}.
As is well known there is a one-to-one
correspondence between set partitions $\pi$ of $[n]$ and equivalence relations
on $[n]$ by defining for $\pi\in\mathcal{P}_n$ and $i,j \in [n]$ the
relation $i \sim_\pi j$ to hold if and only if there is a block $P \in \pi$
such that both $i,j \in P$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
For partitions $\pi$ and $\sigma$ we write $\pi \leq \sigma$ if for any block
$P \in \pi$, there exists a block $S \in \sigma$ such that $P \subseteq S$.  
In other words, every block of $\sigma$ is a union of blocks of $\pi$.
The minimal element of this lattice is
$\hat{0}_n=\{\{1\},\{2\},\dots,\{n\}\}$ and the maximal element
$\hat{1}_n=\{[n]\}$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{app:def:partitions}
   Let $\pi\in\mathcal{P}_n$ be a set partition.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
   \item
    Two (distinct) blocks $B$ and $B'\in\pi$ are said to be \emph{crossing} if
    there are elements $i<i'<j<j'$ such that $i,j\in B$ and $i',j'\in B'$.
    $\pi$ is called \emph{noncrossing} if there are no crossing blocks,
    i.e., if there is no
    quadruple of elements $i<j<k<l$ s.t.\ $i\sim_\pi k$, $j\sim_\pi l$ and
    $i\not\sim_\pi j$.  The noncrossing partitions of order $n$ form a sublattice
    which we denote by $\mathcal{NC}_n$.
   \item\label{item:app:def:partitions2}
    Two blocks $B,B'$ of a noncrossing partition $\pi$ are said to form a
    \emph{nesting} if there are $i,j \in B$ such that $i<k<j$ for any $k \in B'$.
    In this case $B$ is called the \emph{outer block} of the nesting and 
    $B'$ is called the \emph{inner block} of the nesting.
   \item
    A block~$B$ of a noncrossing partition $\pi$ is \emph{inner} if 
    $B$  is the inner block of a nesting of $\pi$.
    If this is not the case $B$ is called an \emph{outer block} of $\pi$.
    The set of inner blocks of $\pi$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Inner}(\pi)$
    and the set of outer blocks of $\pi$ by $\mathrm{Outer}(\pi)$.
   \item
    An \emph{interval partition} is a partition $\pi$ for which every block is an interval.
    Equivalently, this means that~$\pi$ is noncrossing and has no nestings.
    The set of interval partitions of $[n]$ is denoted by $\mathcal{I}_n$. 
    \end{enumerate}
Analogous definitions apply to any finite totally ordered set $A$ and the corresponding sets of partitions are denoted $\mathcal{P}_A$, $\mathcal{NC}_A$, $\mathcal{I}_A$ etc.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- prop-18: body_md -->
\label{app:prop:interval-Boolean}
The lattice of interval partitions $\mathcal{I}_n$ is anti-isomorphic 
to the Boolean lattice $\mathcal{B}_{n-1}$ via the lattice anti-isomorphism
$$
(I_1, I_2, \ldots, I_p) \mapsto\{r_1, r_2, \ldots,r_{p-1}\} \subseteq [n-1],  
$$
where the blocks $I_i$ are uniquely determined by their maximal elements $r_i$;
 note that always $r_p =n$.
<!-- end prop-18 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{app:def:ncmax}
  Fix a number $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and a subset $A\subseteq [n]$. 
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*),leftmargin=1cm]
   \item\label{app:it:outncmax}  Among all noncrossing partitions
  containing $A^c$ as an outer block there is a maximal one, 
  which we denote by $\operatorname{\mathrm{\nu_{\max}}}(A)$. Removing $A^c$ we obtain
  an interval partition of $A$ which we denote by $\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A)$;
  in other words, the blocks of $\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A)$ consist
  of the maximal contiguous subintervals of $A$. 
  Yet in another interpretation, the blocks of $\operatorname{\mathrm{\iota_{\max}}}(A)$ 
  are the connected components of the graph induced on $A$
  from the integer line.
   \item\label{app:it:ncmax}  Among all noncrossing partitions
    containing $A^c$ as a block there is a maximal one, 
  which we denote by $\operatorname{\mathrm{\tilde{\nu}_{\max}}}(A)$. Removing $A^c$ we obtain
  a noncrossing partition of $A$ 
  which we denote by $\operatorname{\mathrm{\tilde{\iota}_{\max}}}(A)$;
  in other words, the blocks of $\operatorname{\mathrm{\tilde{\iota}_{\max}}}(A)$ consist
  of the maximal contiguous subintervals of $A$ when we consider
  it on the circle, i.e.,
